I bought the game when it was released but didn't got into it right away. Seeing so many people get hyped and praise the game everywhere, tumblr being overflowed by fan arts and so many artists on twitter speaking about the game, it sort of made me really reluctent to throw myself into it because everyone just spoke about it to a point it became sickening.
So i left it for some many years, sitting in my "to do" list until i finally felt the need to try it. And so... It left me with a very sour relationship with the game.
Basically, the game is a simple, sort of Mother inspired jrpg where you play as young child falling off a cliff and entering some weird, underground universe inhabited with monsters and puzzles. Although the game plays on these codes and reverse them, amking these monsters more gentle, happy go lucky and in the end, very human creatures with their own problems you have to solve rather than threat you have to kill.
The game is all about systems and code reversal, using a lot of the regular combat encounter interface to create more a way of interracting and conversing with a character more than actually fighting them. Most of the game UI and elements will present its own meta interpretation and lead to some plot twists so i can't really describe much of them without spoiling the fun.
In that spirit, you are quickly taught by the first few character of the game that during thoses encounters, you can solve them either by Fighting (and kill) or Acting (and spare) people, and that it's better act nicely to people rather than be violent and try to kill everyone.
Fight stands up for a more regular jrpg approach with timed attack, where Act will requires you to take the time to read and understand what options presented to you, and how the monster react to it, will let you solve its problem and let you Spare him. It's is very important to understand that you can either Fight or Spare, which is basically the "good or bad" answer to what things will pe presented to you.
It unfortunatly stands up for almost all the moral choices and implications you'll either face during the game if you exclude a few dialogues that you'll be able to answar by A or B here and there, but the writing really makes up for it.
Even if the game lets you explore the area of the underground world, eventually putting you into random encounters, a lot of the core gameplay will be about these encounter, especially for the main plot character you'll encounter that will serve as Boss Fight. Each 'boss' will bring new gameplay elements and so on.
The story itself is pretty straightforward, you will go from a place to another, meeting up a newly introduced character you'll have to face at one point, that once defeated will let you get to know them more, and so on. The game also reveal bits of lore scattered here and there until you reach a certain point where things you'll start to experience will go beyond the simple rules of the game itself.
And honnestly, this works really well. The character are lovable and written in a very beleivable way, a lot of jokes made are kind of sloppy but canon, and all the encounters and small mini game gimmick the game does makes up for an extremly creative take on rpgs and game itself.
So, why did i felt so bad about it ?
Well, from what i understood of my playthrough, the game is about fandoms and how people creates boundaries and defines themselves to others using social medias and being always connected, yet always separated. It speaks about people passions, is inspired by anime and had a lot of details that feels like out of, you know, internet communities, humour and memes you can find on reddit, imgur and tumblr. There's a lot of lgbt friendly character and how the story unfold is pretty much what you'd expect from a regular anime serie but with, sort of born from the western internet culture subject mixed into it. Which isn't a problem at all, far from it.
But the game never really get into questionning its references or putting them into perspective, and instead celebrates it by making you join the fun. Which, for someone who never really got into that kind of internet community or doesn't really understands it, felt really weird and didn't manage to resonate in me the way it did in a more receptive audience.
Also, when the game came out, it inscribed itself in a trend with a couple of other indy games that really made efforts to be self aware and play with the player mind to a point they just tricks and make them realise they were sort of manipulated by their gameplay habits, in order to raise questions into your mind and prove a point to you at the same time. And while i do reckon that this kind of game and plot twists can be mind blowing, i always felt like such plot devices where always tricky and hard to manage if you don't want to break immersion, either being a movie, a book or a game.
To some extent, it really felt like trying to force me to aknowledge how clever the plot twist were by "making me do things i didn't want to" in an almost pretentious way because i never had the choice to do otherwise in the first place. And comparred to games like the stanley parable where you end up playing with the narrator rather than the game, here the game feels more like playing with you instead, which can be really frustrating if you just wanted to, you know, play a game from A to B.
The last thing i also have to complain about is that the game could be really, really hard at time. I mean, i do understand the need to have some challenge in the game and emphasize Determination, so that when you reach past the difficulty it feels rewarding, but here i was really wondering if such tricky difficulty was justified.
My point is that, doing the pacifist run, i spend a lot of my time in the area trying to avoid taking random encounter because most of the time i had to use a lot of healing items just so that once i reach the next 'boss', i wouldn't have to redo the entire sequence just because i didn't do well enough to save my gear. There was also a weird balance between gold earned for sparing people and item prices, which felt really important at time, especially around Mettaton.
It all felt really frustrating just to try to navigate to the next area and be beaten by things you don't want to loose you time with because you're so wanting to reach the next part of the game story. It's sad because the minigame themselve were complelling enough, did it have to be that much hardcore ?
And i only did the peaceful run but, i've heard the violent one is even worse.
But that is just my personnal thought about it.
Truth is that the game is really good. I mean It's fun, it's clever, and really creative more than everything else. It's one of those indy gems that show how leaving people some freedom in the writing can make up for a more thrilling experience than any other big budget, monney worried games you can find in the industry. Just for that i'll totally recommend it to experience it at least once.
I'm just really sad that the over reacting fanbase and other social media trends the game has suffered, coupled with countless spoiler heavy fanart and and posts spoiled the crap out of me and destroyed any sense of intimate experience i could have had otherwise, making up for a weirdly, overly assimilated pop culture thing i could just vaguely consume.

It's a little late for me to make a review for Undertale, but after completing the game for the fourth time, and racking up my play time to over 30 hours (w/o leaving the game on overnight), I felt that I could be a guide for anyone considering this game to buy.
Let me point out many peoples' gripes I see. I hear a lot that people think the game is too short. This in part is true (each run took me about 3-4 hours), but if you decide to do each ending then the game will take a while to "complete". Honestly, the biggest issue I have with this game isn't even the game's fault. The game has so much more of a rich experience if you know NOTHING about it. Going through the whole story clueless about what's going to happen, or what the ending is going to be made this game a hunderd times better.
Now that we have some of the problems out of the way, let's talk about what makes this game so amazing. The price is amazing. If I could get a game for $10 (not on sale) that let me go through an amazing adventure spending over 30 hours, I would do it again every single time. A lot of the tags for the game really show what makes it so great. The game has a magnifient soundtrack, and the reason I haven't bought the soundtrack on Steam for $10 is because it is useless when you can just play any song on YouTube for free. I am not going to potentially spoil the game for anyone, but the game's story is so rich. You feel so attached with the characters, and the world feels really big when it is in fact quite small.  The tags say "choices matter" (again, I'm not going to spoil the story) which the big overarching theme to this game, where the choices you make have an enormous effect on what happens. The game's art at first seems really strange, but as you play through the game more you realize how the art and the music form an amazing atmosphere and mood wherever you go. One thing that is not really a spoiler is telling you how great, and innovative the battle sequences really are. Being given the option to either kill or befreind an enemy with the action segments thrown in makes a huge aspect of the game really unique. There are so many more great things about this game, but I think that just reasons alone would give anyone a good incentive to buy this game.
I can't give a game a ten, ever. I feel that a game is never really perfect, and that I can always pick out some flaws. This game has to get the same treatment though. It does have its cons, but the pros almost completely overshadow those cons. I would have to give the game a 9/10 for the amazing experience it has given me, and not a ten for the sole reason that I wanted it to go on forever!

Borderlands 2 is like a warm slice of apple pie.
Its a majestic ever increasing in difficulty rpg shooter.
Its like an rpg in the sense of making a character unique with looks and skills.
Its a fast paced game that is never short of a dull moment.
The characters have changed since the first but the originals still feature in the game as NPCs.
6 characters in total (2 are dlc)
Salvador the Gunzerker was kind of the flagship character for the game. Everyone was really excited for him and were not disappointed. He is not my typical playstyle however running in as a fast moving dual wielding tank, is impossible not to like.
Axton the Commando, is very similar to Roland. Axton was not exactly a repeat but had a lot of simularities to the previous commando, so he will feel familiar to players of the original commando.
Zero the Assassin, Zero is can either be similar to mordecai or the complete opposite. He has three trees one focuses on sniping and getting huge criticals. His second is called cunning and does exactly what it says. It has benefits for guns and also melee so it is a nice balance of the inbetween. His last focuses on pure melee and lifesteal, he deals massive amount of melee damage to everyone and everything, he is also able to recloak after killing an enemy.
Maya the Siren, is similar and different to Lillith. She focuses on elements as the same as Lillith, but her real difference is her ability. Phaselock, essentially removes the target from the battle lifting them up in the air and freezing them. This can be changed depending on the skill tree that has been chosen. If the target is to large or heavy (usually bosses) it deals significant damage to the bus as a trade off.
Gaige the Mechromancer is very unique. Her ability releases a robot called Deathtrap that wrecks house, he can be upgraded throughout all three trees. She can rebound bullets off walls which is very interesting and entertaining. Anarchy is what one tree focuses on. For every kill and magazine reloaded fdue to no bullets in combat adds 1.75% damage and subtracts the same amount in accuracy. This a source of nearly endless entertainment as you can use whole clip and not hit anyone.
Kreig the Psycho. He is essentially a controllable psycho, thats all that needs to be said.
The game is similar to the first Borderlands, which as we all know is a great thing. The areas are extremely well designed and are extremely plentiful.
I wish this game just didnt end and kept going the story is very well told and implemented well in the game. It is not a game that is essentially an interactive story, it is a difficult game. It is a nice refreshing shooter, that is possibly the best thing to play with a friend. Starting with the game is like a new character is like starting again. It is fairly priced for what you get and the same with the dlc. It is definitely worth getting the game of the year addition from the abundance of the dlc.
I would never not recommend this game to anyone.

I bought the game when it was released but didn't got into it right away. Seeing so many people get hyped and praise the game everywhere, tumblr being overflowed by fan arts and so many artists on twitter speaking about the game, it sort of made me really reluctent to throw myself into it because everyone just spoke about it to a point it became sickening.
So i left it for some many years, sitting in my "to do" list until i finally felt the need to try it. And so... It left me with a very sour relationship with the game.
Basically, the game is a simple, sort of Mother inspired jrpg where you play as young child falling off a cliff and entering some weird, underground universe inhabited with monsters and puzzles. Although the game plays on these codes and reverse them, amking these monsters more gentle, happy go lucky and in the end, very human creatures with their own problems you have to solve rather than threat you have to kill.
The game is all about systems and code reversal, using a lot of the regular combat encounter interface to create more a way of interracting and conversing with a character more than actually fighting them. Most of the game UI and elements will present its own meta interpretation and lead to some plot twists so i can't really describe much of them without spoiling the fun.
In that spirit, you are quickly taught by the first few character of the game that during thoses encounters, you can solve them either by Fighting (and kill) or Acting (and spare) people, and that it's better act nicely to people rather than be violent and try to kill everyone.
Fight stands up for a more regular jrpg approach with timed attack, where Act will requires you to take the time to read and understand what options presented to you, and how the monster react to it, will let you solve its problem and let you Spare him. It's is very important to understand that you can either Fight or Spare, which is basically the "good or bad" answer to what things will pe presented to you.
It unfortunatly stands up for almost all the moral choices and implications you'll either face during the game if you exclude a few dialogues that you'll be able to answar by A or B here and there, but the writing really makes up for it.
Even if the game lets you explore the area of the underground world, eventually putting you into random encounters, a lot of the core gameplay will be about these encounter, especially for the main plot character you'll encounter that will serve as Boss Fight. Each 'boss' will bring new gameplay elements and so on.
The story itself is pretty straightforward, you will go from a place to another, meeting up a newly introduced character you'll have to face at one point, that once defeated will let you get to know them more, and so on. The game also reveal bits of lore scattered here and there until you reach a certain point where things you'll start to experience will go beyond the simple rules of the game itself.
And honnestly, this works really well. The character are lovable and written in a very beleivable way, a lot of jokes made are kind of sloppy but canon, and all the encounters and small mini game gimmick the game does makes up for an extremly creative take on rpgs and game itself.
So, why did i felt so bad about it ?
Well, from what i understood of my playthrough, the game is about fandoms and how people creates boundaries and defines themselves to others using social medias and being always connected, yet always separated. It speaks about people passions, is inspired by anime and had a lot of details that feels like out of, you know, internet communities, humour and memes you can find on reddit, imgur and tumblr. There's a lot of lgbt friendly character and how the story unfold is pretty much what you'd expect from a regular anime serie but with, sort of born from the western internet culture subject mixed into it. Which isn't a problem at all, far from it.
But the game never really get into questionning its references or putting them into perspective, and instead celebrates it by making you join the fun. Which, for someone who never really got into that kind of internet community or doesn't really understands it, felt really weird and didn't manage to resonate in me the way it did in a more receptive audience.
Also, when the game came out, it inscribed itself in a trend with a couple of other indy games that really made efforts to be self aware and play with the player mind to a point they just tricks and make them realise they were sort of manipulated by their gameplay habits, in order to raise questions into your mind and prove a point to you at the same time. And while i do reckon that this kind of game and plot twists can be mind blowing, i always felt like such plot devices where always tricky and hard to manage if you don't want to break immersion, either being a movie, a book or a game.
To some extent, it really felt like trying to force me to aknowledge how clever the plot twist were by "making me do things i didn't want to" in an almost pretentious way because i never had the choice to do otherwise in the first place. And comparred to games like the stanley parable where you end up playing with the narrator rather than the game, here the game feels more like playing with you instead, which can be really frustrating if you just wanted to, you know, play a game from A to B.
The last thing i also have to complain about is that the game could be really, really hard at time. I mean, i do understand the need to have some challenge in the game and emphasize Determination, so that when you reach past the difficulty it feels rewarding, but here i was really wondering if such tricky difficulty was justified.
My point is that, doing the pacifist run, i spend a lot of my time in the area trying to avoid taking random encounter because most of the time i had to use a lot of healing items just so that once i reach the next 'boss', i wouldn't have to redo the entire sequence just because i didn't do well enough to save my gear. There was also a weird balance between gold earned for sparing people and item prices, which felt really important at time, especially around Mettaton.
It all felt really frustrating just to try to navigate to the next area and be beaten by things you don't want to loose you time with because you're so wanting to reach the next part of the game story. It's sad because the minigame themselve were complelling enough, did it have to be that much hardcore ?
And i only did the peaceful run but, i've heard the violent one is even worse.
But that is just my personnal thought about it.
Truth is that the game is really good. I mean It's fun, it's clever, and really creative more than everything else. It's one of those indy gems that show how leaving people some freedom in the writing can make up for a more thrilling experience than any other big budget, monney worried games you can find in the industry. Just for that i'll totally recommend it to experience it at least once.
I'm just really sad that the over reacting fanbase and other social media trends the game has suffered, coupled with countless spoiler heavy fanart and and posts spoiled the crap out of me and destroyed any sense of intimate experience i could have had otherwise, making up for a weirdly, overly assimilated pop culture thing i could just vaguely consume.

It's a little late for me to make a review for Undertale, but after completing the game for the fourth time, and racking up my play time to over 30 hours (w/o leaving the game on overnight), I felt that I could be a guide for anyone considering this game to buy.
Let me point out many peoples' gripes I see. I hear a lot that people think the game is too short. This in part is true (each run took me about 3-4 hours), but if you decide to do each ending then the game will take a while to "complete". Honestly, the biggest issue I have with this game isn't even the game's fault. The game has so much more of a rich experience if you know NOTHING about it. Going through the whole story clueless about what's going to happen, or what the ending is going to be made this game a hunderd times better.
Now that we have some of the problems out of the way, let's talk about what makes this game so amazing. The price is amazing. If I could get a game for $10 (not on sale) that let me go through an amazing adventure spending over 30 hours, I would do it again every single time. A lot of the tags for the game really show what makes it so great. The game has a magnifient soundtrack, and the reason I haven't bought the soundtrack on Steam for $10 is because it is useless when you can just play any song on YouTube for free. I am not going to potentially spoil the game for anyone, but the game's story is so rich. You feel so attached with the characters, and the world feels really big when it is in fact quite small.  The tags say "choices matter" (again, I'm not going to spoil the story) which the big overarching theme to this game, where the choices you make have an enormous effect on what happens. The game's art at first seems really strange, but as you play through the game more you realize how the art and the music form an amazing atmosphere and mood wherever you go. One thing that is not really a spoiler is telling you how great, and innovative the battle sequences really are. Being given the option to either kill or befreind an enemy with the action segments thrown in makes a huge aspect of the game really unique. There are so many more great things about this game, but I think that just reasons alone would give anyone a good incentive to buy this game.
I can't give a game a ten, ever. I feel that a game is never really perfect, and that I can always pick out some flaws. This game has to get the same treatment though. It does have its cons, but the pros almost completely overshadow those cons. I would have to give the game a 9/10 for the amazing experience it has given me, and not a ten for the sole reason that I wanted it to go on forever!

Bought the game when it was in EA, and now I'm definitely placing myself in the "I doubt this will ever get out of EA" camp.
That being said, I can't help but love this game.
(Or maybe I've invested too much of what little playing time I have into this game that I now don't want to admit that I'm dissapointed...)
Anyway, I still find DayZ enjoyable because:
1. The realism. As in, you can't dig metal ores and then craft an assault rifle. This also extends to other gameplay aspects, from the hunger/thirst mechanism, ambient temperature, ballistics, etc., etc. So, playing DayZ mostly feels logical (for lack of a better word... at least it does for me.)
2. The multiplayer. As in, playing with other people can be enjoyable but adventuring solo is viable as well. Which is a big bonus for people like me who can't play on a regular basis.
3. Tension. Approaching an empty-looking village in broad daylight and still having to be careful in case there's somebody with a shotgun also looking around for food; looking at rolling hills carresed by a light summer breeze and worrying about snipers hiding in the forest; etc., etc. These never really get old for me.
Sure, there are a ton of problems, from bugs to glitches and cheaters etc., but I somehow still enjoy loading up the game once in a while to see how far I can make it and what new experiences I can find.

Buy this. It's incredibly fun. It's a good mix of a driving sim, business sim and actual game. So many simulators fall short of providing an experience that is fun. This one delivers. The RPG mechanic is quite addicting. You can level your driver up by completing hauls. Over time, this gives you access to a slew of benefits like unlocking newer, more powerful trucks, as well as upgrades for the in-depth truck garage. You can customize basically anything you can think of on your trucks in this game, from painting it a custom color to changing exterior trim options. You would have to see it to believe how in depth it is. The business side of this game is pretty fun as well, as you can actually hire drivers for your company to haul for you. They give you a percentage once they deliver their goods. You also can buy garages in many of the cities across Europe, expanding your empire and allowing more and more drivers to work for you. The game also has full support for custom music as well as in game internet radio support, making it highly immersive. Buy it!

After having played through it quite a bit. I think I can finally adress a modest opinion of this game.
This game is amazing. While seeming really simple it can be complex and surprising. Replaying the game feels very fresh pretty much every time. The game can be really easy at times while it's also possible to get really hard to punish you for your deeds.
This game is meant for people who've played rpg's before and know at least a bit about geek-culture. Then this is an ultimate experience for a great price.
The soundtrack can seem really simplistic at times but becomes more interesting an lovable as you progress.
The characters are great with each having there own personality that seems really relatable and therefore worth experimenting with through multiple playthroughs.
There are of course some small cons.
-It might scare off some unexperienced gamers because of some unexspected fourth wall breaking.
-The art can be incredibly ugly at times.
Therefore I will give Undertale a 9 out of 10.
Well done Toby Fox. Don't hesitate to ask help from more developers in the future to make the next possible experience worthy of a 10 out of 10.

I got somewhat 250 hours in this game and i just decided to write a review for it.
Game has a lot of potential, some of it hidden. Rust is better played in a group of 3 to 5 on a medium or big server with constant rivals at your doors and glitches on your back. It's been in early access for quite some time now but unlike other games, this one actually has updates (weekly). Devs aren't afraid to change gameplay mechanics to see how it plays out in the end, this is Early Access after all. So, how's the game up close?
Gameplay is simple in its basics. Just survive. Kill, build (optionally, tho, you can even survive without a base), farm (a lot, especially if you're alone) and do whatever you want. Currenly, as of beginning of 2017 there is no end-game content or any specific objective to do. Most people tend to raid once they have reached a certain level of development; some just build the biggest and baddest base around and stay in it, occasionally killing someone from their roof and most of the players are engaged in pvp content, whether they want it or not. No one is protected from having his аss handed to him just because he made a wrong turn in the forest and walked up on a gang of 3 ruskies with ak's and full armor. This is why the game is best played in group, that way you can have an actual objective in game - to have fun together, instead of just building a base or raiding someone.
Graphics, optimisation, all of that are changing constantly and for some the game would be unplayable, but that's only if you have a very old pc. Currenly, i'd have about 40 fps on high on r9 270x and i5. But since it's early access and unity together, means that there are a lot of bugs and nothing can save you if you suddenly freeze during a firefight. Happens occasionally.
Sound - eh, it's alright.
Music - eh, turned it off.
Potential - a lot, if devs keep on updating as they are, game will (probably... hopefully) leave ea with a lot of content and ready to conquer steam charts.

Thought I'd give a go at a honest review for a game for once.
Rust is a interesting game for me. I spent a lot of time on Rust and made many friends. Rust is really unlike other games. It's similar to World Of Warcraft in where people create clans and communities which feeds life into the game. The best way hands down to play Rust is to join a group of friends or people and work together. There are so many intense momments in Rust like your 10 man squad running into another 10 armed guys and having a firefight, knowing you are going to lose all the gear on you if you die. Or taking down a helicopter as a clan and then trying to defend the crash. It's really an intense game unlike any other.
My absolute favourite thing about Rust would be the PvP aspect. It has great shooter aspects. Good netcode and good mechanics. And the devs are constantly balancing it out. The combat rewards skilled shooter players which is awesome. And it's very rewarding to outplay your opponents and collect their gear. It feels good.
Rust survival aspect is great too. Base building is awesome, and the Devs constantly work to improve the game.
You can leave the game for a few months and come back to so many different new additions. The Developers really care beyond many, many other Studios about their product at a level that is really admirable.
So I thought I'd do a overall tally system similar to other reviews at the end:
Postitives:
+ Great PvP
+ Great survival aspects, food, water, tempurature, gathering and farming.
+ Great base-building with many options available
+ Raiding and end-game gameplay is very rewarding and keeps you busy a entire wipe-cylce
+ PvE aspects are great like helicopter fights.
+ Game is constantly developed and improved.
+ Cheaters are handled effectively (now)
+ A social experience similar to MMOS. It's on a completely different level from any first-person shooter style game out there. You can build real friendships that last outside of the game.
Negatives:
- Bears lol
- Offline raiding kind of sucks but is an aspect of the game, this is more of a even aspect. Is has negatives and positives.
- Gameplay can be grindy if you want to play End-game top-tier style all wipe.
- PvP can be unfair as a solo or small group player since there are 10+ people clans roaming severs.
- Performance is very wonky sometimes. It is constantly being improved but still has much room for improvement.
- some other misc things i Can't think of atm.
Overall though I love Rust and I think it's a fantastic game WELL worth the price-tag. I hope this helps you decide on getting the game from the POV of a player that has over 1k hours.

This game is frustrating. Every step is an uphill battle, and the reviews aren't wrong. Everything will kill you. From naked rock wielding 12 year olds to blind deaf bears, to radiation. Every time you begin to do well and feel good about your progress, your base will be raided, and you'll have to start over again, with a rock and a torch on a beach. In the end though, that's what I enjoy about it. While some criticize the lengthy grinding and struggle to succeed, that's what gives the success meaning. That's what makes raids as intense as they are. Knowing that, if the enemy is able to defeat you, weeks of work  go down the drain. This feeling is countered by the glee brought by taking revenge on the group that previously destroyed your work.
Yes, this game has its problems, it has many, but even with them, this game is incredibly enjoyable. Even when you've died 10 times in a row with little to no advancement, something always pulls you back in to respawning again. You'll be hooked the minute you finally build your first house.
Is the majority of the community cancer? Yes. Go into the game knowing that and being prepared for it. I promise you that some of the community is not, and if you are not, you will eventually meet someone who isn't either. It is suggested that you play this game with friends, while I'm sure it is, Rust is most definitely enjoyable without exisiting friends to play it with at the start.
Rust is ever changing, ever evolving, and in my opinion, it looks incredibly promising. I play this game as though this is the final release, and in all honesty, if it were, I would personally be content with it. I see each new update as a welcome and exciting new addition. When this game will have its final release? I have no idea, and I couldn't care less. I really enjoy it for what it is.

The gaming scene is ripe with simulators of various degree and quailty. Most of them are mediocre, some aren't even remotely playable. Usually, they'e just plain silly (yes, "Garbage Truck Simulator", I'm looking at you). Still, when I first stumbled upon the trailer to "Euro Truck Simulator 2", my first thought was not of boredom or even frustration, but rather "how can a game that's main purpose is to drive a truck from point A to B look so cool?".
Somewhere in the perverse dark corners of my deliriousness, I knew, at that moment, that I wanted it. I had to get it. And when most of my friends got hooked, I bought it. And here's the kicker; it is fun. As a trucking simulator, ETS2 is remarkable; you really have full access to all the driving controls (from gearbox to blinker to light setting) and the elements (fuel consumption, tiredness, weather) all have to be accounted for. The driving is easy to handle with a controller (forget keyboard, that'll ruin it for you!) and you really can't botch it up that bad.
That's all fine, but that's not what got it for me. For me, it's the zen-like peacfulness of driving a truck for 30-40 minutes through beautiful landscapes, cities and highways while listening to a streaming radio channel (tweak the SII-file and you can add whatever channel you want!). It's the perfect opposite to the suspense, strategy and action I'm used to; for that, I salute ETS2.
That's what a simulation game should be

We get that the fanbase is bad but the game is good, but that statement is getting really redundant.
Undertale is a superb game, easily being one of my favorites of 2015 (sorry, I havn't played the Witcher series). It's a game with lore, characters, story, and writing all of each are decently developed (with only some flaws in writing when you look deeper into it).
The game has gameplay that stands out from other RPGs by having a combat system that is skill based (being able to dodge enemy attacks by moving your soul), and offers pacifism as a more rewarding option (instead of games you could "theoretically" beat without killing by practically breaking the game, like Fallout or CoD).
The music easily is one of the most memorible parts of the game, offering over a hundred tracks that are bound to keep your ears pleasured.
With all that said, what faults does the game have? There is no run button, making the few times you back-track to be kind of annoying. The game is also locked at 30 fps, which is fine for the overworld, but when in combat I'd prefer a more responsive frame-rate. There are not as many character interactions or development as I'd like. I think an extra one or two hours in length could have fleshed out more of the world and characters, and it could have removed my least favorite part of the game: The giant exposition dump right before a major event in the game. This part felt like a last ditch effort to add more background to a character, due to the dominance in humor over serious moments.
With that all said, the game is a year old, and you probably have heard of it. Despite everything, its still a game worth your money. Undertale will suprise and subvert your expectations in ways wouldn't have seen coming

Ok, this game is amazing. First thing i have to say is YOU DO NOT NEED TO PLAY BORDERLANDS 1 TO FULLY ENJOY THIS GAME.
i can't sum it all up at once so i'm gonna break it down into a couple categories. Skip to the bottom for the ultra quick summarized version.
--THE GUNS--
this game has the world record for the most guns in any game EVER. i dont remember how many there actually are, but once you get past level 5 you can be pretty sure you'll never see the exact same weapon again other than on the loading screens. There are many different kinds of weapons (pistols, rifles, smgs, rocket launchers, shotguns) that you'll find in-game that stronger as you find new ones and level up. Every gun has multiple stats like damage, accuracy, reload speed and so on and your inventory automatically compares the stats of your guns helping you to easily pick and replace guns to take out and sell or keep (gun collection is a big part of this game). the guns also have different type of damage. There are basic bullets like most games have and then theres elemental damage. I'm pretty sure the first element you'll encounter is fire since a really early boss uses it, but eventually you'll see things like electricity, slag (an in game element that, once an enemy hits it, makes them weaker to all other bullet types), caustic(acid), fire and explosive. these elemental damage types can also be dealt through grenades. some of the many side misisons of this game give you exclusive weapons with special effects too but we'll get to that later.
--THE GRAPHICS--
one thing that many people, including me, first saw this game for the graphics and its interesting cell shaded graphic style that many games have tried to copy. It took everything about Borderlands 1's comicy art style and made it smooth and beautiful and it makes all the enviroments in this game's huge world really interesting..speaking of the world..
--THE MAP--
this. game. is. huge. No, its not all exactly one big open world like skyrim, but instead it works in lots and lots of enclosed regions. Every main area in the game (certain towns or enviroments) have their own fast travel that activates when you get to them and then can be used at any time from any other fast travel. This lets you explore the world in a really interesting way because you cant just walk to a new area and encounter any enemies you werent supposed to fight yet and it keeps everything balanced. Even though some of the zones feel small, i still havent explored all the areas after 70+ hours and theres even more if you get the DLC.
--THE CLASSES--
The base game of borderlands 2 has 4 classes that have their own special ability but the great thing about this game's classes is that any class can use any weapon and only the special ability is changed through class. This way everything is accessable for everyone. the classes are these:
COMANDO(Axton): his special is dropping a sentry gun that can be upgraded as you level up to heal you and your team, add extra guns and shoot rockets.
GUNZERKER(Salvador): his special allows him to go into a rage mode and be extra fast while dual wielding guns (no other character dual weilds)
ASSASSIN(ZER0): his special allows him to create a clone of himself to distract enemies and then turn invisible for more stealthy kills
SIREN(Maya)- her special allows her to create a giant ball of energy and suspend the enemy in the air to stun them so they can be shot

the other dlc classes are krieg the psycho and gaige the mechromancer but i dont know much about them
--THE COMBAT--
The combat in borderlands 2 is great. In the beginning, its a simple shooting style. Right mouse to aim, left to shoot etc. but it gets interesting as you level up and think about the games different classes and different weapon types. Every brand of gun in game behaves differently. For example, weapons from Tediore are thrown and exploded when you reload them and a new one appears in your hand. Also some guns have elemental damage which i talked about up above. Once you reach level 5 you can also access your characters rechargable special ability which i talked about up above in the classes section. You also have grenades which can have different effects like elemental and multiplying themselves. Combat becomes more complex as you level up and get further in the game obviously but your health goes up with you and you can collect new stronger sheilds to protect you (they're energy shields that work pretty much like Halo's)
--IMPORTANT!!--
YOU CAN PLAY THIS GAME WITHOUT BORDERLANDS 1. this is a common thing people dont seem to know because it has "2" in the name, but i honestly think its a better entry point to the story anyway. The only thing you'll miss by playing this first is a couple cameos from characters in BL1 but you'll still deeply connect to them (this game has some really strong emotional parts for a comedy fps, especially in the tiny tina dragon keep dlc).
--THE STORY--
The game starts with an opening cutscene summarizing the first game. 4 adventurers on an alien planet named pandora search for the legendary vault, a container said to hold legendary loot. In the end, it turned out the vault was actually an alien prison and the 4 original vault hunters destroyed the beast inside, but without knowing it, opening the vault also released eridium onto the world. eridium is a priceless alien element that completely changed pandora, giving it all new technologies and other advancements. At this time, the evil hyperion corperation came in. They invaded pandora under orders of their leader Handsome Jack, to mine for eridium. The opening cutscene introduces you to the 4 new vault hunters on a train going after handsome jack, but when they get to the head of the train it ends up as a trap with a fake dummy jack rigged with tnt. The train explodes, you land in the snow, CL4P-TP finds you and your adventure begins! Can you find the vault, stop handsome jack and save pandora?
QUICK SUMMARY: THIS GAME IS PERFECT. The side missions have their own mini story lines and there are so many so the game feels endless. The leveling up, combat, and skill point systems are great. The characters and story are funny and sometimes really emotional (dragon keep dlc :( ) The world is amazing and the enviroments are pretty.

This game is frustrating. Every step is an uphill battle, and the reviews aren't wrong. Everything will kill you. From naked rock wielding 12 year olds to blind deaf bears, to radiation. Every time you begin to do well and feel good about your progress, your base will be raided, and you'll have to start over again, with a rock and a torch on a beach. In the end though, that's what I enjoy about it. While some criticize the lengthy grinding and struggle to succeed, that's what gives the success meaning. That's what makes raids as intense as they are. Knowing that, if the enemy is able to defeat you, weeks of work  go down the drain. This feeling is countered by the glee brought by taking revenge on the group that previously destroyed your work.
Yes, this game has its problems, it has many, but even with them, this game is incredibly enjoyable. Even when you've died 10 times in a row with little to no advancement, something always pulls you back in to respawning again. You'll be hooked the minute you finally build your first house.
Is the majority of the community cancer? Yes. Go into the game knowing that and being prepared for it. I promise you that some of the community is not, and if you are not, you will eventually meet someone who isn't either. It is suggested that you play this game with friends, while I'm sure it is, Rust is most definitely enjoyable without exisiting friends to play it with at the start.
Rust is ever changing, ever evolving, and in my opinion, it looks incredibly promising. I play this game as though this is the final release, and in all honesty, if it were, I would personally be content with it. I see each new update as a welcome and exciting new addition. When this game will have its final release? I have no idea, and I couldn't care less. I really enjoy it for what it is.

This game is amazing. Yes, it's just driving trucks around and delivering stuff. Yes, it may be boring for a lot of people, the average gamer in particular. Yes, the graphics aren't the best. Yes, it may be unrealistic at times. But guess what? If you can't get past those facts about this game, and you play games like Forza or Minecraft or Call of Duty, you, my friend, are a hypocrite. Euro Truck Simulator 2 is better than ALL of those games, with the debatable exception of Minecraft. This game is relaxing, scenic, time waisting (in a good way), and just a great activity for most people, even if they aren't a gamer. Graphics and glitches are some pretty unfair aspects to judge this game on. I mean, it's indie. If you can name one indie game that doesn't have outdated graphics and/or tons of glitches, you are amazing. Seriously, in the comments, if you can think of any indie game with good graphics and lacks glitches, let me know. By "good graphics" I don't mean like Terraria where it's supposed to be like that. I mean serious, realistic graphics, like Crysis 3 and other triple-A titles. Anyway, this game is great. It doesn't require a very powerful machine to run, it doesn't take up a lot of hard-drive space. From what I can tell, it simulates driving fairly well, with the mandatory use of headlights and winshield wipers and turn-signals and even road rage. That's right, road rage. The majority of the A.I. are just like those idiot drivers you can find on the road in real life. So, basically, if you don't hate driving, you might enjoy this game. Now, for the price of 40 dollars, that is a bit pricey. I think it could be 25 maybe 30. So if this goes on sale, buy it. You won't regret it.
And one last thing, beware of the Prius.

I got somewhat 250 hours in this game and i just decided to write a review for it.
Game has a lot of potential, some of it hidden. Rust is better played in a group of 3 to 5 on a medium or big server with constant rivals at your doors and glitches on your back. It's been in early access for quite some time now but unlike other games, this one actually has updates (weekly). Devs aren't afraid to change gameplay mechanics to see how it plays out in the end, this is Early Access after all. So, how's the game up close?
Gameplay is simple in its basics. Just survive. Kill, build (optionally, tho, you can even survive without a base), farm (a lot, especially if you're alone) and do whatever you want. Currenly, as of beginning of 2017 there is no end-game content or any specific objective to do. Most people tend to raid once they have reached a certain level of development; some just build the biggest and baddest base around and stay in it, occasionally killing someone from their roof and most of the players are engaged in pvp content, whether they want it or not. No one is protected from having his аss handed to him just because he made a wrong turn in the forest and walked up on a gang of 3 ruskies with ak's and full armor. This is why the game is best played in group, that way you can have an actual objective in game - to have fun together, instead of just building a base or raiding someone.
Graphics, optimisation, all of that are changing constantly and for some the game would be unplayable, but that's only if you have a very old pc. Currenly, i'd have about 40 fps on high on r9 270x and i5. But since it's early access and unity together, means that there are a lot of bugs and nothing can save you if you suddenly freeze during a firefight. Happens occasionally.
Sound - eh, it's alright.
Music - eh, turned it off.
Potential - a lot, if devs keep on updating as they are, game will (probably... hopefully) leave ea with a lot of content and ready to conquer steam charts.

Thought I'd give a go at a honest review for a game for once.
Rust is a interesting game for me. I spent a lot of time on Rust and made many friends. Rust is really unlike other games. It's similar to World Of Warcraft in where people create clans and communities which feeds life into the game. The best way hands down to play Rust is to join a group of friends or people and work together. There are so many intense momments in Rust like your 10 man squad running into another 10 armed guys and having a firefight, knowing you are going to lose all the gear on you if you die. Or taking down a helicopter as a clan and then trying to defend the crash. It's really an intense game unlike any other.
My absolute favourite thing about Rust would be the PvP aspect. It has great shooter aspects. Good netcode and good mechanics. And the devs are constantly balancing it out. The combat rewards skilled shooter players which is awesome. And it's very rewarding to outplay your opponents and collect their gear. It feels good.
Rust survival aspect is great too. Base building is awesome, and the Devs constantly work to improve the game.
You can leave the game for a few months and come back to so many different new additions. The Developers really care beyond many, many other Studios about their product at a level that is really admirable.
So I thought I'd do a overall tally system similar to other reviews at the end:
Postitives:
+ Great PvP
+ Great survival aspects, food, water, tempurature, gathering and farming.
+ Great base-building with many options available
+ Raiding and end-game gameplay is very rewarding and keeps you busy a entire wipe-cylce
+ PvE aspects are great like helicopter fights.
+ Game is constantly developed and improved.
+ Cheaters are handled effectively (now)
+ A social experience similar to MMOS. It's on a completely different level from any first-person shooter style game out there. You can build real friendships that last outside of the game.
Negatives:
- Bears lol
- Offline raiding kind of sucks but is an aspect of the game, this is more of a even aspect. Is has negatives and positives.
- Gameplay can be grindy if you want to play End-game top-tier style all wipe.
- PvP can be unfair as a solo or small group player since there are 10+ people clans roaming severs.
- Performance is very wonky sometimes. It is constantly being improved but still has much room for improvement.
- some other misc things i Can't think of atm.
Overall though I love Rust and I think it's a fantastic game WELL worth the price-tag. I hope this helps you decide on getting the game from the POV of a player that has over 1k hours.

I have to say I didn’t really enjoy the game all that much. One nickname for the game on the Internet is “Snorederblands 2,” and that’s because of the game’s essential “Diablo with guns” gameplay: that is to say, endless waves of repetitive enemies which drop incrementally more effective loot that you can use to power up your character. Sounds awesome in theory, but in practice you get tired of facing the same five or six groups of enemies for 40 hours rather quickly.
A lot of the thrill of such a game comes from its incremental rewards: finding a neat piece of loot when you kill a difficult boss or open an obscure chest. However, Gearbox (the creators of “Borderlands”) introduced a system in “Borderlands 2” that completely circumvented the need to find loot. They added a “Golden Chest” in the middle of the main city that you could open for rare and powerful items — more powerful than anything you would find in an initial playthrough. To open this chest you need “Golden Keys” which are acquired by entering codes from social media into a special dialog box buried in the “Extras” menu. The problem is, Gearbox left a lot of the codes active for the life of the game, and they have long since been collected on various websites for anyone to use. Combine that with HiddenSamurai’s almost weekly notifications that new codes were available, and I opened the Golden Chest 5 - 10 times with every level that I gained, and I think I still have over 150 keys left. It totally removed the incremental reward system from the game, which was sort of a bummer.
The dialogue and humor of the game is often frequently mentioned as a strong point, and while I found it amusing, it never really “clicked” with me to the point where I found it hilarious. It seemed to verge almost completely on “Internet humor” with death and mayhem and memes. Human life is a cheap trifling thing in a game like Borderlands. But, I guess that’s true for all video games.
I was playing as the melee-centric character “Krieg” the “Psycho,” and once I got his ultimate “Mania” tree power — the ability to grow twice in size and deal out twice as much melee damage — I started to have a lot more fun. I stacked a bunch of other bonuses with my various skills and items so at the end I think I had something like 600% melee damage, when raging. I was doing 100 - 105K in melee strikes by the end of the game, probably nothing compared to a level capped character, but it seemed like a lot to me, at level 36. Combined with the 50% damage reduction I got while raging, I was basically an unstoppable maelstrom of death as long as I found a good place to retreat to once it wore off.
My room-mate played as “Maya” the “Siren” character, who specializes in healing and/or crowd control. Unlike myself, who stuck with one build through the whole game, he shifted around his skill points as the situation demanded, or as whim struck him. He is a far more skilled gamer than I am, regularly getting 2.0 K/D in Call of Duty matches, so his effectiveness with a sniper rifle was very useful. He also eventually got the ultimate skill, a “battle res” that could instantly revive me from death, which was useful when I could charge into a situation a little over my head.
All-in-all I’d give “Borderlands 2” a hesitant “thumbs up,” and a rating of three stars out of five. I enjoyed my time with it, but due to its repetitive nature I could really only stomach it in segments of an hour to two hours of play.

Borderlands is one of those game series that you'll get a lot of different a opinions on. Some people love it, some people hate it. Some people really want to like it, but they can't force themselves to. For me, it's a near-perfect game with some extremely frustrating elements.
To break it down into simple terms, I love the art style, the characters, and the satirical direction Gearbox went with it. Claptrap is funny to me, even if he is the JarJar Binks of video games, your silent protagonist is always spoken to directly, but seems to be peripheral to the whole thing. You are, after all meant to be that character.
The special powers are fun and combat is a blast. No matter how many times you die, you can always retry failed missions and just respawn. This is normal, but it's stlil pretty cool in this game because they do give you a penalty for it. You have to pay some money. The more money you have, the more money they take. This is what motivates you to not die, but you will die a lot. Even still, it's a game that Gearbox obviously wants you to win.
My playtime isn't a joke, it's literally 50 hours of me being obsessive. If you have been accurately diagnosed with obsessive compulsive disorder by a physician, it's probably not the type of game you want to play. My only major complaints are usually the same complaints I have with games - the soundtrack is cool for a little while, but it grows really tired after just an hour or so. Maybe I'm unique in this, but a full soundtrack is maybe 2 hours of music, and I fail to see how Gearbox couldn't afford someone to compose thise considering game music creators are a dime a dozen. If they put real money into that, it's a waste.
However, the voice acting is near-flawless and some of what they say is hilarious, most of it being just chuckleworthy. There are parts that will have you running in circles that make the game feel a bit repetitive, to a degree. But that's not a totally bad thing with Borderlands 2, because you'll always be picking up some neat loot and weapons.
One thing you'll never have to actually buy is weapons, but sometimes the "daily specials" at the vending machines are pretty good, so make sure you check them out. The mini games and joke missions are also enjoyable, and they cause you to sympathize with some of the characters even while there's a lot of humor behind their destruction or self-loathing.
The DLC thing is divisive. I did buy all the DLC's for content, and I personally think they were worth it.
In short, you'll get out of this game exactly what you put into it. It can take you 8 hours, or it can take you 800 hours. I don't think you'll find any shortage of real gameplay here.

The gaming scene is ripe with simulators of various degree and quailty. Most of them are mediocre, some aren't even remotely playable. Usually, they'e just plain silly (yes, "Garbage Truck Simulator", I'm looking at you). Still, when I first stumbled upon the trailer to "Euro Truck Simulator 2", my first thought was not of boredom or even frustration, but rather "how can a game that's main purpose is to drive a truck from point A to B look so cool?".
Somewhere in the perverse dark corners of my deliriousness, I knew, at that moment, that I wanted it. I had to get it. And when most of my friends got hooked, I bought it. And here's the kicker; it is fun. As a trucking simulator, ETS2 is remarkable; you really have full access to all the driving controls (from gearbox to blinker to light setting) and the elements (fuel consumption, tiredness, weather) all have to be accounted for. The driving is easy to handle with a controller (forget keyboard, that'll ruin it for you!) and you really can't botch it up that bad.
That's all fine, but that's not what got it for me. For me, it's the zen-like peacfulness of driving a truck for 30-40 minutes through beautiful landscapes, cities and highways while listening to a streaming radio channel (tweak the SII-file and you can add whatever channel you want!). It's the perfect opposite to the suspense, strategy and action I'm used to; for that, I salute ETS2.

I played through the game basically at the insistence of my room-mate, who claimed it was one of his favorite games, and that he has beaten it more than five times. He also couldn’t get any of his other friends to play it anymore, it being a rather old game which was released in 2012. Nearly every time he and I both shared some free time, he would be pestering me to play this game. So, desirous of something which we could enjoy in common, I agreed.
I have to say I didn’t really enjoy the game all that much. One nickname for the game on the Internet is “Snorederblands 2,” and that’s because of the game’s essential “Diablo with guns” gameplay: that is to say, endless waves of repetitive enemies which drop incrementally more effective loot that you can use to power up your character. Sounds awesome in theory, but in practice you get tired of facing the same five or six groups of enemies for 40 hours rather quickly.
A lot of the thrill of such a game comes from its incremental rewards: finding a neat piece of loot when you kill a difficult boss or open an obscure chest. However, Gearbox (the creators of “Borderlands”) introduced a system in “Borderlands 2” that completely circumvented the need to find loot. They added a “Golden Chest” in the middle of the main city that you could open for rare and powerful items — more powerful than anything you would find in an initial playthrough. To open this chest you need “Golden Keys” which are acquired by entering codes from social media into a special dialog box buried in the “Extras” menu. The problem is, Gearbox left a lot of the codes active for the life of the game, and they have long since been collected on various websites for anyone to use. Combine that with HiddenSamurai’s almost weekly notifications that new codes were available, and I opened the Golden Chest 5 - 10 times with every level that I gained, and I think I still have over 150 keys left. It totally removed the incremental reward system from the game, which was sort of a bummer.
The dialogue and humor of the game is often frequently mentioned as a strong point, and while I found it amusing, it never really “clicked” with me to the point where I found it hilarious. It seemed to verge almost completely on “Internet humor” with death and mayhem and memes. Human life is a cheap trifling thing in a game like Borderlands. But, I guess that’s true for all video games.
I was playing as the melee-centric character “Krieg” the “Psycho,” and once I got his ultimate “Mania” tree power — the ability to grow twice in size and deal out twice as much melee damage — I started to have a lot more fun. I stacked a bunch of other bonuses with my various skills and items so at the end I think I had something like 600% melee damage, when raging. I was doing 100 - 105K in melee strikes by the end of the game, probably nothing compared to a level capped character, but it seemed like a lot to me, at level 36. Combined with the 50% damage reduction I got while raging, I was basically an unstoppable maelstrom of death as long as I found a good place to retreat to once it wore off.
My room-mate played as “Maya” the “Siren” character, who specializes in healing and/or crowd control. Unlike myself, who stuck with one build through the whole game, he shifted around his skill points as the situation demanded, or as whim struck him. He is a far more skilled gamer than I am, regularly getting 2.0 K/D in Call of Duty matches, so his effectiveness with a sniper rifle was very useful. He also eventually got the ultimate skill, a “battle res” that could instantly revive me from death, which was useful when I could charge into a situation a little over my head.
All-in-all I’d give “Borderlands 2” a hesitant “thumbs up,” and a rating of three stars out of five. I enjoyed my time with it, but due to its repetitive nature I could really only stomach it in segments of an hour to two hours of play.

Torino to Edinboro' on a 6x2 Truck. The lull as you slowly drift from on ramp, to motorway and back off again. You pass through cardboard copies of cities, but you don't care cause youre relaxed.
You drive through Germany.
You see a city with the same layout as the previous, AI lorries cut you up at 60MPH and Oncoming traffic spawns just as you've commited yourself to a three car overtake on a long straight.
You curse, slam on the brakes and ease back into the traffic. You get a fine for speeding and being on the wrong side. Thanks Gamelogic.
Before you know it, youre at Dover. You roll off the ferry and are instantly greeted with a 90 Degree turn left, but the turning circle isnt wide enough and there are central reservation barriers on both the exit lane and entry point.
You execute the fabled 324 Point turn, whilst incurring £2,000 in Cargo damage, £1,650 in collision fees and £650 for pressing F7 for roadside assistance.
Edinboro'. You pull into the yard, instantly remember the kerfuffle you had with the 324 point turn and proceed to repeat it for the parking maneuvre.
You conceed defeat and press Enter to auto park.
Then you do it ALL over again, because its so damn relaxing. Did I mention that?

So for those of you not knowing really what it is basically your a truck driver going across europe and little further with the dlc.
You first start out doing missions for other companies because you don't have enough money to buy your own truck, but once you do they give you a garage where you can bascially run your business by hiring drivers and getting trucks for them to drive. It's not really that deep but they help you earn money as you get better drivers and more trucks and so on.
It has quite a few settings for controllers, mouse and keyboard, and steering wheels. You can change it to automatic, true automatic (which is when you change it from neutral to drive/reverse), manual, and sequiential (spelled that wrong) which i think is true manual, i havent used because i don't have a steering wheel. I've used a keyboard and mouse and its ok not the greatest but if you dont have any other option than it's still playable, but i highly suggest controller/steering wheel.
Now for gameplay, the trucks handle great, a scania (saab) won't handle the same as a volvo truck it will have a completely different feel for it. Many different camera angles but the best is cockpit view. Traffic isn't the best but its not horrible they don't usually cut you off but they will brake pretty hard for no reason sometimes. Then there is this thing where you trying to get on the freeway and you have traffic getting off the freeway and it will just be a cluster ♥♥♥♥ basically where you are just stuck and have to illegal manuevering to get out of there. Also you have to get gas and sleep, there is damage to your truck, speeding tickets, red light tickets and crashing into cars penalties. There isn't police so don't worry about getting pulled over, and you don't have to get out of your truck to pump gas it isn't a super sim either.
There really isn't a endgame to this so don't expect it, it basically drive here collect cargo drop off cargo, buy more trucks, buy garages. Also has a ranking up system. But still don't let that pull you off the game is great, the driving the rig seeing the europing countryside, (not really much detail of the cities). Its just an amazing game, buy it if you haven't its an amazing game that everybody should play just to experience what trucking is about. Without all the boring paperwork trucking has in real life.
TL:DR - ETS2 does the simulation right and also has the enjoyment of an actual game. Buy it

Borderlands 2 is a exciting loot fest to enjoy with your friends, and then some. BL2 brought out some things I would never expect nor imagine with what it showed us at E3.
Borderlands 2 is exactly what you would want out of a Borderlands game - over the top and GUNS GUNS GUNS. You have weapon variety that is exciting and fresh. You have enemies that are scary as hell to entertaining as hell. But Borderlands 2 hides something that I would have not asked for, nor expected from its game - its a damn good RPG.
I was suprised to find that character skill trees are deep and engaging, with much room for experimentation. Much like the emotional appearence of the Bordlerands 2 characters, their skills define them and change how you play your class. For example, my Mechromancer can't manually reload unless I want to lose anarchy stacks, which increase my damage. This applies for every character, which has its own interesting playstyle and role.
If I had a complaint about the game, it would be that the story is not good. While the characters might be hilarious and are definatley interesting, the "plot twists" and progression aspect aren't that cool. With the adventure that you are on, it is easy to lose track and forget your purpose for the adventure.
Might I also add that the missions are fun?!?!!?! They are just like the skill trees - fresh and exciting. While you get the occasional fetch, you will also find great missions backed by humourous settings and backstory.
Borderlands 2 exceeded my expectations. I not only got an over the top experience, but a very in depth and methodical one. Considering the low prices this game constantly gets thanks to good old Gaben, this game is a blast with a couple of friends.

Borderlands 2 is a very mixed bag. At times, it can be incredibly fun, as you unload shotgun pellets into Psycho Midget faces and throw buzz axes at a Goliath's head. At other times, it can be an incredibly tedious game as you backtrack from place to place and are forced to perform some infurating timed quests. The same can be said for its juvenile sense of humor. At times, it can be a very funny game, but at plentyof other times, you'll groan at how dumb a joke was or how awful a reference was.
Let's get the biggest issue out of the way first. This game is terribly boring in the first couple of hours. You barely have any variety in combat, you have very few and very weak weapons, and you don't really have any interesting quests. It's a slog through the campaign until you get enough skill points in your character to make the game fun. For example, in my playthrough as Krieg the Psycho, it was a boring experience until I got enough points in cooldown reductino to let me spam my active ability freely.
And on that note, we look at another big flaw of Borderlands 2: the skill tree. Every character gets only one active skill, such as being able to dual wield guns, turn invisible, or summon a giant mech of death. While this improves the variety of combat greatly at first, you don't get any of the more interesting or game changing abilities until your character is at a very high level (31 or more). Until then, you're stuck with (mostly) boring percentage stat boosts that barely affect your playstyle. To the game's credit, there are a hanful of interesting skills that do change how you play significantly, but there aren't enough of them. If there was more than one active skill, then the skill tree would be a little more tolerable, but as it stands, it's a grind to get the skills that you actually want.
Next on the chopping block is the music and gun sounds. The guns, more often than not, sounds incredibly weak. You often feel like you're firing a peashooter, not a quad barreled shotgun. It's all incredibly underwhelming, to be honest. The music is fine, but it does a very poor job of pumping your adrenaline. That is, the music never helps you feel like the badass that the game wants you to be.
My next major complaint is the loot system, in that it's not very good. There are some interesting weapons and drops, but more often than not, you'll get crappy guns that you'll just throw away because they're too weak or underleveled. This wouldn't be so bad if guns scaled to your current level, but since they don't, you'll be getting a lot of trash in proportion to useful equipment.
Also, the performance of this game is not very consistent. At times, I can get 120 FPS no problem, but when I turn 180 degrees, it become a quarter of what it was a second ago. After trying numerous engien tweaks and reducing graphical fidelity, not much improves the performance of this game (I run a 780 Ti, so it's a very capable rig). It's not a dealbreaking, but it is very annoying.
Finally, the story is very threadbare, despite Gearbox's efforts to improve it this time around. The entire story can be summed up to: Handsome Jack is a♥♥♥♥♥♥ go kill Jack. I mean, the story does its job in getting you from place to place and ferrying you to a wide variety of locales, but it really isn't anything memorable.
So, now onto the good.
The combat can be really fun late game when your character is properly specced out. Having a maxed out Mania tree in Krieg is a blast as you one shot enemies with your melee weapon or snipe them from afar with your thrown buzz axes. You'll eventually get some interesting guns that have some very powerful effects that mesh with your playstyle or change it up.
Co-op is pretty seamlessand allows you to drop into and out of a friend's game quickly. Enemies will become tougher, and loot will become better, so it's definitely the way to play if you have a couple of good buddies.
The voice acting, in general, is very well done. Solid deliveries by the cast all around, and there are some very well delivered lines (pretty much anything by Handsome Jack is well voiced, for example). There really aren't any characters that get get on your nerves, unless you find Ashley Burch's voice grating.
Finally, the game can be incredibly funny in its own stupid way. If you embrace the cheese of the game and accept stupid jokes like "bonerfarts", then you're going to have a good time. However, it should be known that this game relies entirely on crass humor, so if you don't like that sort of thing, you will not enjoy the humor whatsoever.
So, in conclusion, Borderlands 2 is a very slow burner because of its poor skill tree and loot system, but it picks up later on in the game as you get more interesting loot and skills. It's definitely great as a co-op game, but it's a fun experience too if you play solo.

Ok, I have an insane amount of hours in this game. I've played it since they changed North East Airfield and removed the tents. People that complain about the game have a pretty cynical idea of what an alpha release game is. From the time I started playing, the game has vastly improved. If you don't believe me then please download experimental and give it a try.
As far as slow development, I can only speculate. I have a pretty good idea that they have had to nearly  re-write all the code since aquiring it from Dean Hall's crew. That is no small feat. Now that they have introduced the Enfusion engine and the audio improvements and fixed the character animations so that your avatar no longer dies from stairs or rocks the game has greatly improved.
They have changed a number of the cities, added bases, updated the zombies, introduced wolves and overall have been plugging in updates extremely quickly. Of course they aren't continuing to develop the current non-experimental because that would be stepping backwards.
Survival is the genre of the game and if you can't understand that then by all means buy yourself CSGO and die/respawn endlessly. Dayz was not meant to be a PVP game, it's a mix of PVE and PVP. It is entirely unscripted and offers completely random experiences everytime you play. I've met incredible people and amazing trolls. To this day I still play with some of the people I met when I first purchased the game and we have a blast.
I can honestly say I've never had a game give me adrenaline rushes like DayZ and I'm excited to see what changes are in store and for the mod-ability that is coming.
Keep up the good work!

Driving a truck can be as engaging and fun as any other game out there, you just need to give it a chance first. A game where the basic concept is simple, you drive your truck from point a to point b, get rewarded with money and continue on with future jobs, but where other simulators fail to hook the player, Euro Truck Simulator 2 manages to do the job right.
This is not your average driving a truck simulator, in it you actually get to upgrade your vehicle, upgrade your character, level up, customize almost anything on your truck and even start your own company where you can hire other people to drive your trucks and make money for you. But hey, if you don't feel like doing any of that, there's always random jobs up on the job board from people that have a truck and need you to do a delivery, after you finish the job you return the truck and get your money, nothing more and nothing less, so this way I find it extremely easy to get into and just enjoy.
Driving for great distances can sometimes be associated with "boring" which is not the case at all here. I find this to be the most relaxing game I have ever experienced, often times playing a couple of podcasts at the radio, sit back and enjoy a long drive, there's nothing like it really and you can't bash it till you try it, trust me. Time in the game is compressed, so for example, a 10 hour drive in real life will be about a 40-60 minute drive in the game, this is for a couple of reasons, but mainly to get you engaged on as many roads as possible, to admire everything it has to offer!

I'm a great fan of the Arma 2 DayZ Mods and bought this game almost THREE years ago with great expectations and with absolute certainty that it will be finished in a short time. Well, now I'm here, three bloody years later and the game is still in Early Access and looks like utter crap. It was the first Early Access game I ever bought and it is the reason that I don't buy them anymore unless my friends convince me that a certain game is REALLY worth it (which only happened once).
DayZ Standalone is the amalgamation of all reasons why you shouldn't buy Early Access games and it really deserves the title of "How to take a popular name and squeeze the most money out of a loyal community but don't give them anything in return". Let's be serious, how hard can it be to take all the great ideas and concepts from the DayZ mods (which people developed for free in their spare time) and put it into one game with better graphics? But no, all we ever got was a game with a broken engine and a laughable development progress over a period of THREE years. I really believed in this game and wanted to give the devs a chance but for me the time has come to say enough is enough.
TL;DR: If you want to have the DayZ experience buy Arma 2 and play the mods! But don't waste your money on this sorry little freak that stole the glorious name of some of the best mods I ever played in my life!
