After more than 200 hours of gameplay (which were totally worth it) on all three game mods through numerous side missions and DLCs, I have few things to say about this game. Like, it's awesome!
It was a great idea to combine a FPS with an RPG in case of Borderlands, it's even more so with Borderlands 2. Compared to its predecessor, Borderlands 2 has a lot of improvements: better graphics, better characters, more convenient interface, easier loot picking (money and ammo is picked automatically, by walking over them), more DLCs, more humor, more various enemies, more maps, more action, better skill trees.
I think what makes Borderlands 2 such a great game and a must-have, is its unique setting of Pandora with its outlaws, monsters and dark politically incorrect humour.
However, there are some things that are annoying and/or disappointing.
1. Loot system: 98% of weapons and equipment are crap. All great or just decent weapons are rare. The unique reward weapons often are worse than the regular weapons that you have already equiped. Also, in Borderlands 2 there are only 5 million weapon combinations, whereas in Borderlands there are 17 million combinations. With that said, a lot of time is spent on comparing and sorting weapons, which at some point becomes frustrating. I wish there were some kind of automatic recommendations that could help save time. Well, there is a colour system – orange weapons and purple weapons should theroretically be the best, but that's not always the case. I think a filter system would be handy, when a player can set preferences for potential loot.
2. Side missions: some of the side missions are really stupid, like ''go there and pick X number of things'' or ''walk a skag (sort of a dog-like monster) for 5 mins not killing it''. Such missions are typical in RPG games, but in my opinion this should have been one RPG aspect Gearbox should have skipped. Also, a major part of side missions has a very weak storyline or no storyline at all.
3. Maps: some might disagree, but I personally hate these serpentine-like maps with endless turns and hidden passages. Also, it's hard to locate a target in a monochromatic, schematic representation of a multi-level area in a mini-map. You have to guess on which level the target actually is, e.g., in a cave or on a cliff, on the ground floor or rooftop. I'd prefer if the distance would be indicated as in Assassin's Creed.
4. Fast travel stations: you travel distance and between maps either by vehicles or using fast travel stations. As a result, lots of time is spent by either running or driving and fighting the enemies you had already killed before. I'd rather prefer an outpost system as in FarCry 3.
5. Vehicles: often it's much easier to be a pedestrian. Besides, the vehicle guns are weak and impractical.
6. Unbalanced leveling and enemies. Apart from Ultimate Vault Hunter mode, in which you face enemies who are two levels higher than you and quite hard to kill, in Normal Mode and True Vault Hunter mode, you mostly face weak enemies and around level 30 further leveling becomes annoyingly slow, since the experience gained is ridiculously small but the necesssary amount of experience points gets higher and higher with each level. Also, I don't think that there should be a level cap (which is 72 with the second upgrade pack), because some of the bosses in the Ultimate Vault Hunter Mode are of level 80 - that means that you can't possibly kill them.
7. This game is pushing Co-Op, because some of the missions are so hard, it's almost impossible to beat the game in single-player - you just get tired of dying and wasting expensive ammo on hordes of enemies.
8. Finally, I don't think that it's fair that all the DLCs are not included in the Season Pass or GOTY edition. With the exhausting level-ups and search for legendary weapons, it's just plain exploitation of players. It's a sort of corporate behaviour you would expect from EA and Ubisoft.
Although there are points when Borderlands feels just like a pointless loot grab and desperate skill tree development, it is one of my top favourite games. I hope the Borderlands Presequel would be even better.
9/10.

Alright, everybody's here? Great. Time to begin my review.
Borderlands 2 is an FPS whose gameplay moreso leans towards RPG aspects, having classes with their respective skill trees, quests, levels based on experience progression and gear (equipment) being a key role. Each class has a unique action skill which changes gameplay for each class to a certain extent. As you progress in the game, you will be building your character to favour your playstyle, and likewise for your gear as well. Builds get fairly deeper as you gain higher levels. These RPG aspects of the game are good and alot of fun, but not the best and could surely be improved on.
Gear is primarily similar to those in (MMO)RPGs. Mobs have loot tables and the harder the enemy, the more likely for them to drop better and more loot. This has its perks and weaknesses to the game considering if you absolutely hate grinding for good gear and the RNG gods dont smile upon you that often, then you would have kind of a bad time. But when you get a really good gun which you may fall in love with, then it truly is a glorious feeling. Guns are another key aspect to the game as there are literally a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of them and you'd be lying if you did not like any one of them as the guns are a hell lot of ridiculous fun.
Story in Borderlands 2 is good, but not great. BUT (notice the big BUT there), the writing in this game is nothing short of perfect. The dialog, setting and scripted events are an absolute match made in heaven and anyone (except those who are easily offended) could easily fall in love with it at first sight. This inevitably leads to a strong team of unforgettably loveable characters due to the game's over-the-top narrative and setting. If there is one reason to play it, it is for that reason.
In short, mix in a game with excellent but not-so-perfect gameplay, with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of loot and guns with fun mechanics, a ridiculously over-the-top premise set in outer space full of people with questionable sanity and some of gaming's strongest, most unforgettable characters, and you get Borderlands 2, a game I could really recommend to anyone as it is a blast to experience.
OH and multiplayer is absolutely, balls-out, insane fun especially if you're playing with your mates.

Ok, I have an insane amount of hours in this game. I've played it since they changed North East Airfield and removed the tents. People that complain about the game have a pretty cynical idea of what an alpha release game is. From the time I started playing, the game has vastly improved. If you don't believe me then please download experimental and give it a try.
As far as slow development, I can only speculate. I have a pretty good idea that they have had to nearly  re-write all the code since aquiring it from Dean Hall's crew. That is no small feat. Now that they have introduced the Enfusion engine and the audio improvements and fixed the character animations so that your avatar no longer dies from stairs or rocks the game has greatly improved.
They have changed a number of the cities, added bases, updated the zombies, introduced wolves and overall have been plugging in updates extremely quickly. Of course they aren't continuing to develop the current non-experimental because that would be stepping backwards.
Survival is the genre of the game and if you can't understand that then by all means buy yourself CSGO and die/respawn endlessly. Dayz was not meant to be a PVP game, it's a mix of PVE and PVP. It is entirely unscripted and offers completely random experiences everytime you play. I've met incredible people and amazing trolls. To this day I still play with some of the people I met when I first purchased the game and we have a blast.
I can honestly say I've never had a game give me adrenaline rushes like DayZ and I'm excited to see what changes are in store and for the mod-ability that is coming.
Keep up the good work!

Let's be serious, how hard can it be to take all the great ideas and concepts from the DayZ mods (which people developed for free in their spare time) and put it into one game with better graphics? But no, all we ever got was a game with a broken engine and a laughable development progress over a period of THREE years. I really believed in this game and wanted to give the devs a chance but for me the time has come to say enough is enough.
TL;DR: If you want to have the DayZ experience buy Arma 2 and play the mods! But don't waste your money on this sorry little freak that stole the glorious name of some of the best mods I ever played in my life!

Soundtrack is great, graphics and art style are fitting, characters have personalities, the game gives you choices, the story is complex...
Great. All of that is great.
But how's the gameplay?
My problem with Undertale is the gameplay. There are bad parts in other areas, like the bad jokes or morality system, but what made me stop playing is the gameplay. There are three parts to it- Attacking, Sparing, and Bullet Hell.
Attacking: To put it simply, attacking is boring. Click the Fight button, hit somewhere on the eye (which decides your damage), and that's it. The only differences in attack animations are between weapons (and even then, some share animations). It gets boring after a while- maybe having different animations for the same weapon would have helped, but the actual act of fighting and killing feels dull and impersonal, causing the game's attempts at guilt tripping to fail (but more on those later).
Sparing: This is actually fun. It works like a sort of dialogue puzzle- selecting the right options in the right order to convince your opponent to stop fighting. The only problem with it is certain characters (usually bosses) whose sparing methods are unusual or convoluted (looking at you Undyne).
However, sparing your enemies creates a larger problem. Killing enemies gets you exp to increase your level, like in any other RPG. But, sparing enemies doesn't get you exp, meaning that your stats don't increase and you end up fighting powerful enemies with low stats. This leaves you with a choice- either get really good at bullet hell, or go back and start farming.
Bullet Hell: It's a decent idea- it makes combat more involving and gives you a chance to avoid damage without using a random number generator. My problem with it is that enemies' attacks can come from all directions and rarely have a pattern, making it difficult for anyone with little experience in bullet hells.
There is one other problem I have with the game- its message. The game attempts to subvert normal video game tendencies (specifically the tendency to fill areas with cannon fodder enemies that no one cares about) by giving every single character a personality and by having the other characters in the game world respond to their deaths. I have a few problems with this idea:
1: The enemies are attacking YOU. Every person I killed was killed in self defense- THEY started the battle. Why are random people traveling through a wilderness attacking me? I have no idea!
2: The enemies are abnormal for video games. Yes, they look like monsters, but they're actually normal travelers which, in most other video games, would be non-hostile or even impossible to kill. Usualy video games have you fighting hostile wildlife, undead/demons/etc., or bandits/similar violent criminals. Video games rarely ask you to just kill everyone, and those you shouldn't kill- Little Sisters, traveling merchants, etc.- are clearly indicated as such, and there is often a punishment for killing them.
3: The game fails to make you feel responsible for the killings. Call me a heartless ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, but the only time I felt any remorse for killing someone in this game was Toriel (and even then it was a "Huh. That was sad" not a "OH GOD I'M SO SORRY [loud crying]). Nothing else in the gamemade me feel even remotely sad. Some, like Papyrus and Undyne, even left me with a feeling of "Serves them right".
I think that, since video games are an interactive medium, gameplay should come first over story or messages. And the unique story that this game tells can't come close to salvaging its poor gameplay and faulty message.

When this little game rolled onto the Steam storefront on September 15th of 2015, I think it’s pretty safe to say hardly anyone probably could’ve imagined the impact it would have. I know I certainly didn’t; after all, my first exposure to Undertale came in the form of seeing the backlash its own fanbase brought upon it, alongside the vocal cynics and critics who panned it as “overrated garbage”. With claims flying left and right that it was the next Five Nights At Freddy’s and constant jokes about how it was “Tumblr’s favorite game”, I had plenty of reason to be skeptical.
When I looked into things myself, though, I found something far different than what I had been anticipating. Even from the very first moments I saw it in action, Undertale…connected with me, in a way few games have ever managed to, first impression or otherwise. As time continued on, I was shocked to see just how much love the game was receiving, including praise from such people as Totalbiscuit and Yahtzee (people known to have trouble enjoying most JRPGs), and so it rapidly became clear that there had to be something to this game; something big. If it could so thoroughly draw in even those who typically can’t enjoy the genre, then if nothing else, it had to be worth checking out.
I went in with some damn high expectations.
What I got was one of the best games I’ve ever played.
I truly wish I had the words to properly explain what Undertale is to me. I could go on for hours about the near-perfection of the soundtrack. I could rave about the writing and how rewardingly rich in detail and nuance it is. I could praise it for its characters and the level of care put into making even the most minor NPCs come to life with personality. I could write a freakin dissertation on the sheer brilliance of how it uses meta not only to comment on the tropes and conventions of its genre, but also as a powerful gameplay and storytelling tool that rewards replay value. I could gush until the end of time about the powerful messages Undertale presents and the skill with which it presents them, even addressing real world issues with an inspiring amount of dignity.
However, what I truly adore the most about this game is how unapologetic it is. It’s never afraid to be what it is, and that confidence takes its strengths and makes them into something far greater than the sum of those parts. From start to finish, Undertale is one of the most utterly brilliant games I’ve ever seen, executed with a pitch-perfect prowess that creates an experience the likes of which few other games can match.
There is always something new; another layer to be peeled back; another beautiful detail to be discovered. And the deeper one digs, the more brilliantly this absolute diamond of a gem sparkles. No part of Undertale is manufactured: not a single pixel has escaped the loving caress of a gentle crafting hand, and as the offspring of a mere $51,000 Kickstart (over 10x the amount Toby asked for), it’s easily one of the most refreshing games of the last few years. Undertale made me laugh. Undertale made me cry. Undertale made me think deeply about the world around me.
But most powerfully of all, Undertale touched me unlike any game before it. It's no small wonder, then, that upon completion it became my favorite game that I've ever played.
Yes indeed, this wonderfully unforgettable experience.
It fills me.
With determination.
I adore this game.

Driving a truck can be as engaging and fun as any other game out there, you just need to give it a chance first. A game where the basic concept is simple, you drive your truck from point a to point b, get rewarded with money and continue on with future jobs, but where other simulators fail to hook the player, Euro Truck Simulator 2 manages to do the job right.
This is not your average driving a truck simulator, in it you actually get to upgrade your vehicle, upgrade your character, level up, customize almost anything on your truck and even start your own company where you can hire other people to drive your trucks and make money for you. But hey, if you don't feel like doing any of that, there's always random jobs up on the job board from people that have a truck and need you to do a delivery, after you finish the job you return the truck and get your money, nothing more and nothing less, so this way I find it extremely easy to get into and just enjoy.
Driving for great distances can sometimes be associated with "boring" which is not the case at all here. I find this to be the most relaxing game I have ever experienced, often times playing a couple of podcasts at the radio, sit back and enjoy a long drive, there's nothing like it really and you can't bash it till you try it, trust me. Time in the game is compressed, so for example, a 10 hour drive in real life will be about a 40-60 minute drive in the game, this is for a couple of reasons, but mainly to get you engaged on as many roads as possible, to admire everything it has to offer!

Hmm... I like and don't like Borderlands 2. Borderlands is something of a series that requires multiplayer, but without multiplayer the game simply doesn't work. Which is a shame because there are multiplayer games out there that can stand on their own as a solo experience, and are only enhanced with multiplayer, which I think is preferable (Divinity: Original Sin, Portal 2, etc).
The writing's funny, the game looks cool, the weapons are cool, it's all fun. But it tends to get long in the tooth very quickly, which is why your friends running around and using bizzare weapons and doing cool tricks is a requirement. The quests are creative, but they aren't a long strong draught of narrative, and most can (and will) be skipped. The game also throws a million tiny quests out there, so you and your friends can vaguely stumble in a direction, guns ablazing, and accidentally come to some sort of a conclusion.
But don't take that as a sleight, THAT'S where the game is. I personally wish the questing aspect was a tighter and more immersive experience. Pandora is a world that's begging to be explored, but paradoxically the game does everything in it's power to leave you with a shallow immersive experience. I guess the devs assumed it would get in the way of the gameplay, and I can see that.
Regardless, really really really good game. Buy it, buy all the DLC, buy all the extra clothing for every character and PLAY this game! Yes, even if you suck at FPS, just play the Mechromancer, one of the best designed character classes ever in the history of anything.

Frankly, I bought Borderlands 2 just last summer sale cos it was pretty damn cheap and was pretty much thinking of playing it abit and probably not picking it up ever again after a couple of hours since I don't really enjoy most open world FPS's that much coming from an avid MMORPG player background.

Alright, everybody's here? Great. Time to begin my review.
Borderlands 2 is an FPS whose gameplay moreso leans towards RPG aspects, having classes with their respective skill trees, quests, levels based on experience progression and gear (equipment) being a key role. Each class has a unique action skill which changes gameplay for each class to a certain extent. As you progress in the game, you will be building your character to favour your playstyle, and likewise for your gear as well. Builds get fairly deeper as you gain higher levels. These RPG aspects of the game are good and alot of fun, but not the best and could surely be improved on.
Gear is primarily similar to those in (MMO)RPGs. Mobs have loot tables and the harder the enemy, the more likely for them to drop better and more loot. This has its perks and weaknesses to the game considering if you absolutely hate grinding for good gear and the RNG gods dont smile upon you that often, then you would have kind of a bad time. But when you get a really good gun which you may fall in love with, then it truly is a glorious feeling. Guns are another key aspect to the game as there are literally a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of them and you'd be lying if you did not like any one of them as the guns are a hell lot of ridiculous fun.
Story in Borderlands 2 is good, but not great. BUT (notice the big BUT there), the writing in this game is nothing short of perfect. The dialog, setting and scripted events are an absolute match made in heaven and anyone (except those who are easily offended) could easily fall in love with it at first sight. This inevitably leads to a strong team of unforgettably loveable characters due to the game's over-the-top narrative and setting. If there is one reason to play it, it is for that reason.
In short, mix in a game with excellent but not-so-perfect gameplay, with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of loot and guns with fun mechanics, a ridiculously over-the-top premise set in outer space full of people with questionable sanity and some of gaming's strongest, most unforgettable characters, and you get Borderlands 2, a game I could really recommend to anyone as it is a blast to experience.
OH and multiplayer is absolutely, balls-out, insane fun especially if you're playing with your mates.
9/10, 11/10 when multiplayer (seriously, its really really fun in multiplayer.)
Amazing. RPG+FPS=Borderlands 2

But how's the gameplay?
My problem with Undertale is the gameplay. There are bad parts in other areas, like the bad jokes or morality system, but what made me stop playing is the gameplay. There are three parts to it- Attacking, Sparing, and Bullet Hell.
Attacking: To put it simply, attacking is boring. Click the Fight button, hit somewhere on the eye (which decides your damage), and that's it. The only differences in attack animations are between weapons (and even then, some share animations). It gets boring after a while- maybe having different animations for the same weapon would have helped, but the actual act of fighting and killing feels dull and impersonal, causing the game's attempts at guilt tripping to fail (but more on those later).
Sparing: This is actually fun. It works like a sort of dialogue puzzle- selecting the right options in the right order to convince your opponent to stop fighting. The only problem with it is certain characters (usually bosses) whose sparing methods are unusual or convoluted (looking at you Undyne).
However, sparing your enemies creates a larger problem. Killing enemies gets you exp to increase your level, like in any other RPG. But, sparing enemies doesn't get you exp, meaning that your stats don't increase and you end up fighting powerful enemies with low stats. This leaves you with a choice- either get really good at bullet hell, or go back and start farming.
Bullet Hell: It's a decent idea- it makes combat more involving and gives you a chance to avoid damage without using a random number generator. My problem with it is that enemies' attacks can come from all directions and rarely have a pattern, making it difficult for anyone with little experience in bullet hells.
There is one other problem I have with the game- its message. The game attempts to subvert normal video game tendencies (specifically the tendency to fill areas with cannon fodder enemies that no one cares about) by giving every single character a personality and by having the other characters in the game world respond to their deaths. I have a few problems with this idea:
1: The enemies are attacking YOU. Every person I killed was killed in self defense- THEY started the battle. Why are random people traveling through a wilderness attacking me? I have no idea!
2: The enemies are abnormal for video games. Yes, they look like monsters, but they're actually normal travelers which, in most other video games, would be non-hostile or even impossible to kill. Usualy video games have you fighting hostile wildlife, undead/demons/etc., or bandits/similar violent criminals. Video games rarely ask you to just kill everyone, and those you shouldn't kill- Little Sisters, traveling merchants, etc.- are clearly indicated as such, and there is often a punishment for killing them.
3: The game fails to make you feel responsible for the killings. Call me a heartless ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, but the only time I felt any remorse for killing someone in this game was Toriel (and even then it was a "Huh. That was sad" not a "OH GOD I'M SO SORRY [loud crying]). Nothing else in the gamemade me feel even remotely sad. Some, like Papyrus and Undyne, even left me with a feeling of "Serves them right".
I think that, since video games are an interactive medium, gameplay should come first over story or messages. And the unique story that this game tells can't come close to salvaging its poor gameplay and faulty message.

When this little game rolled onto the Steam storefront on September 15th of 2015, I think it’s pretty safe to say hardly anyone probably could’ve imagined the impact it would have. I know I certainly didn’t; after all, my first exposure to Undertale came in the form of seeing the backlash its own fanbase brought upon it, alongside the vocal cynics and critics who panned it as “overrated garbage”. With claims flying left and right that it was the next Five Nights At Freddy’s and constant jokes about how it was “Tumblr’s favorite game”, I had plenty of reason to be skeptical.
When I looked into things myself, though, I found something far different than what I had been anticipating. Even from the very first moments I saw it in action, Undertale…connected with me, in a way few games have ever managed to, first impression or otherwise. As time continued on, I was shocked to see just how much love the game was receiving, including praise from such people as Totalbiscuit and Yahtzee (people known to have trouble enjoying most JRPGs), and so it rapidly became clear that there had to be something to this game; something big. If it could so thoroughly draw in even those who typically can’t enjoy the genre, then if nothing else, it had to be worth checking out.
I went in with some damn high expectations.
What I got was one of the best games I’ve ever played.
I truly wish I had the words to properly explain what Undertale is to me. I could go on for hours about the near-perfection of the soundtrack. I could rave about the writing and how rewardingly rich in detail and nuance it is. I could praise it for its characters and the level of care put into making even the most minor NPCs come to life with personality. I could write a freakin dissertation on the sheer brilliance of how it uses meta not only to comment on the tropes and conventions of its genre, but also as a powerful gameplay and storytelling tool that rewards replay value. I could gush until the end of time about the powerful messages Undertale presents and the skill with which it presents them, even addressing real world issues with an inspiring amount of dignity.
However, what I truly adore the most about this game is how unapologetic it is. It’s never afraid to be what it is, and that confidence takes its strengths and makes them into something far greater than the sum of those parts. From start to finish, Undertale is one of the most utterly brilliant games I’ve ever seen, executed with a pitch-perfect prowess that creates an experience the likes of which few other games can match.
There is always something new; another layer to be peeled back; another beautiful detail to be discovered. And the deeper one digs, the more brilliantly this absolute diamond of a gem sparkles. No part of Undertale is manufactured: not a single pixel has escaped the loving caress of a gentle crafting hand, and as the offspring of a mere $51,000 Kickstart (over 10x the amount Toby asked for), it’s easily one of the most refreshing games of the last few years. Undertale made me laugh. Undertale made me cry. Undertale made me think deeply about the world around me.
But most powerfully of all, Undertale touched me unlike any game before it. It's no small wonder, then, that upon completion it became my favorite game that I've ever played.
Yes indeed, this wonderfully unforgettable experience.
It fills me.
With determination.
I adore this game.

Borderlands 2 is a very mixed bag. At times, it can be incredibly fun, as you unload shotgun pellets into Psycho Midget faces and throw buzz axes at a Goliath's head. At other times, it can be an incredibly tedious game as you backtrack from place to place and are forced to perform some infurating timed quests. The same can be said for its juvenile sense of humor. At times, it can be a very funny game, but at plentyof other times, you'll groan at how dumb a joke was or how awful a reference was.
Let's get the biggest issue out of the way first. This game is terribly boring in the first couple of hours. You barely have any variety in combat, you have very few and very weak weapons, and you don't really have any interesting quests. It's a slog through the campaign until you get enough skill points in your character to make the game fun. For example, in my playthrough as Krieg the Psycho, it was a boring experience until I got enough points in cooldown reductino to let me spam my active ability freely.
And on that note, we look at another big flaw of Borderlands 2: the skill tree. Every character gets only one active skill, such as being able to dual wield guns, turn invisible, or summon a giant mech of death. While this improves the variety of combat greatly at first, you don't get any of the more interesting or game changing abilities until your character is at a very high level (31 or more). Until then, you're stuck with (mostly) boring percentage stat boosts that barely affect your playstyle. To the game's credit, there are a hanful of interesting skills that do change how you play significantly, but there aren't enough of them. If there was more than one active skill, then the skill tree would be a little more tolerable, but as it stands, it's a grind to get the skills that you actually want.
Next on the chopping block is the music and gun sounds. The guns, more often than not, sounds incredibly weak. You often feel like you're firing a peashooter, not a quad barreled shotgun. It's all incredibly underwhelming, to be honest. The music is fine, but it does a very poor job of pumping your adrenaline. That is, the music never helps you feel like the badass that the game wants you to be.
My next major complaint is the loot system, in that it's not very good. There are some interesting weapons and drops, but more often than not, you'll get crappy guns that you'll just throw away because they're too weak or underleveled. This wouldn't be so bad if guns scaled to your current level, but since they don't, you'll be getting a lot of trash in proportion to useful equipment.
Also, the performance of this game is not very consistent. At times, I can get 120 FPS no problem, but when I turn 180 degrees, it become a quarter of what it was a second ago. After trying numerous engien tweaks and reducing graphical fidelity, not much improves the performance of this game (I run a 780 Ti, so it's a very capable rig). It's not a dealbreaking, but it is very annoying.
Finally, the story is very threadbare, despite Gearbox's efforts to improve it this time around. The entire story can be summed up to: Handsome Jack is a♥♥♥♥♥♥ go kill Jack. I mean, the story does its job in getting you from place to place and ferrying you to a wide variety of locales, but it really isn't anything memorable.
So, now onto the good.
The combat can be really fun late game when your character is properly specced out. Having a maxed out Mania tree in Krieg is a blast as you one shot enemies with your melee weapon or snipe them from afar with your thrown buzz axes. You'll eventually get some interesting guns that have some very powerful effects that mesh with your playstyle or change it up.
Co-op is pretty seamlessand allows you to drop into and out of a friend's game quickly. Enemies will become tougher, and loot will become better, so it's definitely the way to play if you have a couple of good buddies.
The voice acting, in general, is very well done. Solid deliveries by the cast all around, and there are some very well delivered lines (pretty much anything by Handsome Jack is well voiced, for example). There really aren't any characters that get get on your nerves, unless you find Ashley Burch's voice grating.
Finally, the game can be incredibly funny in its own stupid way. If you embrace the cheese of the game and accept stupid jokes like "bonerfarts", then you're going to have a good time. However, it should be known that this game relies entirely on crass humor, so if you don't like that sort of thing, you will not enjoy the humor whatsoever.
So, in conclusion, Borderlands 2 is a very slow burner because of its poor skill tree and loot system, but it picks up later on in the game as you get more interesting loot and skills. It's definitely great as a co-op game, but it's a fun experience too if you play solo.

For a game that's intentionally for a younger audience, I found this very fun and sometimes surprisingly challenging. This probably shouldn't come as a surprise though since it takes much of it's gameplay influence from the Bullet Hell genre. You could say this game has popularized the genre since Bullet Hell I consider to be a pretty niche genre.
The highlight of the game for me was the Mettaton segment, I found that entire area very fun.
This game offers a fun unique story, great gameplay, and the fact that it is replayable is an understatement.
I was impressed with how well your actions take real effective concequences in this game, something done so well I think Bethesda should really be envious.
When I first started this game, I was frustrated by how the game encouraged the pacifist approach, feeling that it was the game that would not let me play it. But as I got further into the game, I realized that the real heart of the gameplay is the passive approach. Figuring out characters holds a lot more depth than just mindlessly attacking them, and that's the beauty of this game! It truly is.
Unfortunately, I feel this game lacks in proper level design. Your sent on a linear quest through a shallow (but beautiful) world experiencing jokes disguised as puzzles. One of this game's biggest flaws is how it sometimes tries too hard to be funny that it kind of dominates the experience overall.
Either way, this was a great experience and I'm glad to have beaten this. One of these days I'm certain to try the other two routes this game offers if anything just to experience the extra bosses and content.
This game deserves a sequel, but I'd say it would probably be difficult to make story wise. But who knows what the creator might come up with. He's certainly very creative.

First off, I see a lot of negative reviews from players that have played this game from a very early stage and they seem to be quite butthurt. I don't know about this "Legacy"-thing, but if the game is as different as the old players says then the reviews aren't representative for what the game is today.
That being said, here's my thoughts on the game:
It's fun. Before me and my GF bought the game we were hesitant because of the mixed reviews. But after a good couple of hours in the game we realised that we couldn't stop playing. Every aspect of the game was enjoyable as i saw it. Collecting, crafting, building, socialize, hunting and even getting killed as a "fresh-spawn" was an element of the game that made it exciting/interesting.
Seeing all the huge fortresses and bases that other players have built made us realise that we could never get to that point due to our lack of regular activity (because we are both university students). Luckily there are many detailed guides one google-search away on how to host your own server. I will not mention in this game how much more "fun" it is to play with friends.  If a game cannot be fun on its own, then it is not a fun game.  Adding friends to the mix is fun, because being with your friends is inherently fun.  It does not make the game better.
This game shows to be pretty promising.  The developers promised uncompromising support for the PC, and they delivered on it.  The PC options are robust and you can customize practically everything, from the HUD location to the FOV to how good the textures look.  I like the art style and the setting, but both of those things are pretty subjective for the most part.
As for the gameplay, this is where the game kind of falls flat.  There are 4 playable classes (without buying the DLC.. the DLC adds 2 more) and each one has a unique ability.  Salvador, the Gunzerker's special ability allows him to use two weapons at the same time.  Maya's lets her suspend an enemy in mid-air, and if it can't be lifted, it does massive damage, and so on.
The whole problem I have with Borderlands is that it tries to feel like Diablo, with the constant, unending loot quest. In that regard, it succeeds, and much better than its predecessor.  It still lacks vital elements, however: there's no direct customization of a gun.  If you don't like that this weapon has a scope, YOU CAN'T CHANGE IT.  If you want your faithful shotgun to use electricity-firing ammo, well YOU CAN'T CHANGE IT.  Maybe there's something like this in the DLC, but as far as I know, there isn't, because I wasn't willing to buy DLC for a feature that should have been included at level 1.
This game, like a typical Diablo-style game, has boss fights.  The problem with the boss fights is that they typically feel really unfair.  A boss is essentially just one gigantic enemy with unfair levels of health and damage.  Their attacks, even if telegraphed, often cannot be dodged.  So you may frequently find yourself fighting a boss that becomes a battle of attrition: you keep throwing yourself at the boss until eventually it dies.  Now, maybe you find that fun.  I don't.
The characters are really uninteresting, with really Family Guy-esque humor ("Lol, his name is Butt Stallion because he's a walking horse's butt") as well as Anthony Burch attempting to insert sexuality into the game in an attempt to seem "progressive," when all it does is come off as contrived and annoying.  "Oh, this character's bisexual?  Alright, then, but how does that help me shoot things?"
This game could have benefitted from a lot of things, but overall I guess it's okay.  I never beat it because I just got so bored eventually of the endless grind of fighting absurd numbers of enemies, beating down their numbers, and then eventually beating them.  Hooray.

I have played DayZ mod for a very long time, pretty much from the beginning. I had loads of fun, met many friends and repeatedly stayed long hours, thinking that I will play 'just 5 more minutes'.
DayZ Standalone was supposed to be a step-up from the limited engine of Arma II. It was supposed to give us more options, more resources and a completely new degree of fun.
In the first few months, despite the game being in Early Access, I have indeed had lot of fun playing it with friends. The clothing system, new animations and engine, it all proved to be something new and exciting.
Unfortunately, after a month of playing heavily, we stopped. Why ? Because the game was repetitive, and stagnant. The many updates and new resources promised by the game creators turned out to be lies, and dreams.
Sadly, the devs let us down many times. The grand plans, the groundshaking ideas they spouted, turned out to be nothing more than empty promises. In a way, they reminded me of Peter Molyneux. He too promised grand games, great dreams, that in the end turned out to be nothing more than pipe dreams.

I will not mention in this game how much more "fun" it is to play with friends.  If a game cannot be fun on its own, then it is not a fun game.  Adding friends to the mix is fun, because being with your friends is inherently fun.  It does not make the game better.
This game shows to be pretty promising.  The developers promised uncompromising support for the PC, and they delivered on it.  The PC options are robust and you can customize practically everything, from the HUD location to the FOV to how good the textures look.  I like the art style and the setting, but both of those things are pretty subjective for the most part.
As for the gameplay, this is where the game kind of falls flat.  There are 4 playable classes (without buying the DLC.. the DLC adds 2 more) and each one has a unique ability.  Salvador, the Gunzerker's special ability allows him to use two weapons at the same time.  Maya's lets her suspend an enemy in mid-air, and if it can't be lifted, it does massive damage, and so on.
The whole problem I have with Borderlands is that it tries to feel like Diablo, with the constant, unending loot quest. In that regard, it succeeds, and much better than its predecessor.  It still lacks vital elements, however: there's no direct customization of a gun.  If you don't like that this weapon has a scope, YOU CAN'T CHANGE IT.  If you want your faithful shotgun to use electricity-firing ammo, well YOU CAN'T CHANGE IT.  Maybe there's something like this in the DLC, but as far as I know, there isn't, because I wasn't willing to buy DLC for a feature that should have been included at level 1.
This game, like a typical Diablo-style game, has boss fights.  The problem with the boss fights is that they typically feel really unfair.  A boss is essentially just one gigantic enemy with unfair levels of health and damage.  Their attacks, even if telegraphed, often cannot be dodged.  So you may frequently find yourself fighting a boss that becomes a battle of attrition: you keep throwing yourself at the boss until eventually it dies.  Now, maybe you find that fun.  I don't.
The characters are really uninteresting, with really Family Guy-esque humor ("Lol, his name is Butt Stallion because he's a walking horse's butt") as well as Anthony Burch attempting to insert sexuality into the game in an attempt to seem "progressive," when all it does is come off as contrived and annoying.  "Oh, this character's bisexual?  Alright, then, but how does that help me shoot things?"
This game could have benefitted from a lot of things, but overall I guess it's okay.  I never beat it because I just got so bored eventually of the endless grind of fighting absurd numbers of enemies, beating down their numbers, and then eventually beating them.  Hooray.
This is a great shooter and is excellent in multiplayer.  Level disparity is quickly evened out.

When I first saw this game, I went into it thinking, "it's odd that this game has alot of hype, but I don't see why," and that is when it all started. I absolutely LOVE this game, aside from SOME of the fandom, altogether, it's an amazing experience, and I highly reccommend both playing it, and playing it with no info on the game what so ever. Sadly, I didn't have this advantage, as I watched the game before I played it. But I may as well give my experience/opinion on the game.
Undertale is a game where no one has to die (as it says in the description.) YOU choose which path you take, if it's for the better, or worse. It has a really simple battling system, and quite mediocre graphics, (even if it's suppose to be a throw back to the 8-bit games, which I will admit, I don't really enjoy, but I still think of it as "mediocre"), but an amazing story.
I have never been more impressed seeing a game like this, THIS is how you make a game where you have choices. Being a friendly pacifist will end up with nobody getting hurt, and everyone as your friend. Being a genocidal maniac will end up with everyone leaving, they're scared of you, they don't want to see you! Unlike some other story driven games...
Mostly, the story is the thing that I love, although playing really hard battles is fun, because I enjoy a challenge, the story is jaw-droppingly good. (Is that a word? Oh well, it is now! XD).
Not only that, but the soundtrack is also really good. Personally, my favourite would be Your Song That Spear of Spider Heart His Megalotrousl- I CAN'T PICK ONE!!

I also like the humour, yes, it is full of memes, puns (ESPECIALLY PUNS), and twitter jokes, but... IT'S FUNNY TO MEEEEEE.

WARNING.  THIS REVIEW CONTAINS SPOILERS FOR THE GAME.
Undertale.
The game is indescribable.  Now I will describe it to the best of my abilitys:
Its emotional, halarious and very well put together.  It will make you laugh, and it will make you cry.  It is one hell of a game.
First I want to talk about the story.
Undertale's story is one of the best game stories I have EVER seen.  And even though I'm a teenager, I've played games a-many and Undertale is by far one of the best.  The way Toby-Fox had written it makes you really “become one” with the universe of the game.  Characters break the fourth wall and make you laugh while you end up crying during the pacifist route from leaving goat-mom.
Having been made by just one guy, it’s very impressive.  The characters are also so well written it has you falling in love within second of meeting them.  One time literally.  It makes you really question morals, in game and out.
The story isn’t linear, and all decisions you make in one run affect your next one.
The soundtrack is what really ties the whole game together in the end. 101 songs of pure DETERMINATION.  A song for every situation and a situation for every song.  Each song fits the scene and makes you feel a certain way.  While Megalovania makes you feel pumped up and dread at the same time, Home makes you feel emotional and cared for.  Premonition makes you suspicious of true intentions and Once Upon a Time sets the scene.  What I really appreciate that Toby did is that he re-used parts of songs (motifs) so you would feel familiar with the characters and story as time went on.  You could hear Bonetrousle and say “Hey!  I recognize that song!  That’s Papyrus’ song!  This must be his boss battle!”  The soundtrack is over all amazing and its worth buying the game just to hear it used.
Overall I rate the game 10/10 for being what it is.  Perfect games don’t exist, and everything has its flaws.  Undertale is the closest to a perfect game I have ever seen.   Kudos to Toby-Fox for creating something to be loved by generations to come.  The game is timeless and can be replayed over and over.
I hope you buy the game and support Toby-Fox because this man is a legend and has created something wonderful.

Давайте расскажу в чем смысл игры.
Игра основано на том, что бы выжить. Настал "Зомби апокалипсис" и человек управляя своим аватаром должен как можно дольше дней прожить (в конечном итоге он все равно умрет, но не так ли и в реальной жизни?). Игра на столько реализована под реальную жизнь что ты в нее прям проникаешь и чувствуешь как буд то ты и есть твой аватар.
Графика у игры очень хорошо проработана, но для этого и нужен хороший комп. Так же авторы игры позаботились над тем что бы человек у которого слабый комп все равно мог поиграть в нее на минимальных настройках.
Ваш аватар очень капризный как настоящий человек, он постоянно хочет есть и пить и если его не покормить или не напоить то он умрет, а так же он может заразится вирусом или отравиться. Есть море вещей которые вы можете найти в разных частях карты, так же куча людей которые так и хотят тебя убить и забрать весь твой лут (лут это вещи).
По моему мнению главный враг в этой игре не зомби так как их там как кот наплакал, а такие же люди как и вы, но авторы игры обещали это исправить, как ни как игра про " Зомби - Апокалипсис".
В скором времени так же появятся машины, и не просто автомобили раскиданные по всей карте как допустим в ГТА, а настоящая редкость которая будет постоянно ломаться и просить бензин.

I break this game into 2 aspects. There is the ‘exploration, puzzle, and story segments of the game which take the best elements of the Earthbound series and run with them. It pushes defensive combat into little ‘arcade-like’ sections that will have you dodging bullet hells and scrambling to survive the next hit. WARNING.  THIS REVIEW CONTAINS SPOILERS FOR THE GAME.
Undertale.
The game is indescribable.  Now I will describe it to the best of my abilitys:
Its emotional, halarious and very well put together.  It will make you laugh, and it will make you cry.  It is one hell of a game.
First I want to talk about the story.
Undertale's story is one of the best game stories I have EVER seen.  And even though I'm a teenager, I've played games a-many and Undertale is by far one of the best.  The way Toby-Fox had written it makes you really “become one” with the universe of the game.  Characters break the fourth wall and make you laugh while you end up crying during the pacifist route from leaving goat-mom.
Having been made by just one guy, it’s very impressive.  The characters are also so well written it has you falling in love within second of meeting them.  One time literally.  It makes you really question morals, in game and out.
The story isn’t linear, and all decisions you make in one run affect your next one.
The soundtrack is what really ties the whole game together in the end. 101 songs of pure DETERMINATION.  A song for every situation and a situation for every song.  Each song fits the scene and makes you feel a certain way.  While Megalovania makes you feel pumped up and dread at the same time, Home makes you feel emotional and cared for.  Premonition makes you suspicious of true intentions and Once Upon a Time sets the scene.  What I really appreciate that Toby did is that he re-used parts of songs (motifs) so you would feel familiar with the characters and story as time went on.  You could hear Bonetrousle and say “Hey!  I recognize that song!  That’s Papyrus’ song!  This must be his boss battle!”  The soundtrack is over all amazing and its worth buying the game just to hear it used.
Overall I rate the game 10/10 for being what it is.  Perfect games don’t exist, and everything has its flaws.  Undertale is the closest to a perfect game I have ever seen.   Kudos to Toby-Fox for creating something to be loved by generations to come.  The game is timeless and can be replayed over and over.
I hope you buy the game and support Toby-Fox because this man is a legend and has created something wonderful.

This is a charmingly dumb romp, with generally enjoyable gunplay and character skills.  I found the overall story and end boss confrontation to be significantly better than the original.
The main questline is generally pretty fun and sufficiently novel, but many of side missions are mind-numbling boring and tedious, so much so that I skipped many of them (particuarly those that I out-leveled).  I would much have rather seen a reduction in the number of side missions, so long as it mean an increase in their quality, inventiveness, and (where appropriate) length.
I also felt that some of the missions were poorly balanced, almost necessitating that you outlevel them before trying, at least on the higher difficulties, which further exacerbacted the tedium.  The crass and juvenille humor does get old after a while, but I suppose it's no mystery what we've signed up for here.  And of course, the inventory system is needlessly terrible. Again.
TL;DR: Fun, somewhat better than the original, but still with all of the same strenghts and faults, depending of course on how you define terms.  Pick it up on a firesale, and get the Season Pass if you're a die-hard.

Borderlands 2 is the bombastic sequel to the original Borderlands game; it offers improvements over its predecessor along with a new story, characters and environments to provide a game that is bigger and better in every way.
Firstly, the story consists of the villain, Handsome Jack, attempting to access the Vault in order to control the all-powerful Warrior, which will allow him to eliminate any resistance on Pandora. You play as one of four Vault Hunters, who are tasked with defeating Jack and bringing peace to the planet. Axton (the Commando), Salvador (The Gunzerker), Maya (The Siren) and Zer0 (The Assassin); these four classes offer different sets of abilities and perks, and all catered to suit different playing styles. The different skills possessed by each character means you'll definitely want to attempt multiple playthroughs to get a grasp of the 4 characters.
Many of the characters are quirky and entertaining to interact with; this is because of the smart dialogue and strong voice work of all characters involved in the game. Handsome Jack is especially entertaining, as his dialogue stays funny throughout the entirety of the game.
The gameplay is intended to be a blend of RPG's and traditional shooters, dubbed the action-rpg. You'll play in first person and use iron sights just like any other shooter, but there are RPG elements such as inventory management, skills/perks, levelling, and the obviously large in-game map. There are plenty of things to do such as side-quests and even exploration, to allow the player to level up as well as accessing new kinds of loot. There is a large amount of content included in this game, meaning that the player will devote 50+ hours if they are keen on 100% completion.
There is a ridiculous amount of guns to collect, all with differing statistics and appearances. The sheer amount of guns constantly varies the gameplay, and you'll be constantly looting new weapons and exchanging them for your old ones. I liked how the game encouraged you to actively search for new guns, and it would reward you for doing so.
Finally, the game looks and runs great. The stunning environments and large colour palette made the game stand out amongst other games released in the same time frame; this was a much-needed improvement of the bland arrangement of colours included in the previous game.
Overall, Borderlands 2 is a ridiculously satisfying game. The sheer amount of content in addition to the polished game mechanics, story and graphics means that this is a game you'll have no problem putting hours into. Heavily recommended for fans of first-person shooters and standard role-playing games. 9 / 10.

The most overrated game I've ever played; probably my favorite game ever right now.
(this is going to sound a lot like my Skyrim review, and I might come back and change things later - spoiler free, though!)
It's a charmer, for sure, and I can see why. Just in the first room or two it introduces you to its cutesy retro art style, its nostalgic and catchy music, its memorable characters, its unique battle system, and its gut-wrenching twists. But it is absolutely not a perfect or flawless game.
The art is - well, I'm not really sure what it's trying to be. I think it's supposed to be reminiscent of third-generation home console games, but it's fairly sophisticated for that. The overworld art is just plain ugly: thick black outlines everywhere, no or inconsistent shading, broken perspective, no textures or detail, lines that look like they were drawn freehand with a touchpad in Microsoft Paint, usually only three frames per animation (if you're lucky! Most NPCs are actually completely static). In contrast, the backgrounds and shopkeepers have some absolutely gorgeous pixel art! Though, again, it would really fit in more with fourth-gen stuff with the expanded color palette. In between those extremes, then, is the battle screen, which is only in black and white. It's boring, but it works. The battle screen artwork has nice detailing and animations. What really irks me is its use of this pixel art in combination with liberal scaling, rotation, and transparency effects, which absolutely do not fit the aesthetic, do not always look good, and would not have been technically feasible on third- or fourth-gen consoles. Like, if you were going to do fancy stuff like that, why even bother with the fake upscaling?
The music is catchy and intelligently composed, but not really well produced. It mixes chiptune-like music with tracker-style stuff and even a bit of live instruments and faked full orchestration. Which, on the surface, I'm fine with. I love me some fakebit. But, going back to the whole retro-aesthetic thing, it doesn't match any retro console it's trying to emulate. It's also a bit annoying that the soundtrack just tries to use generic-sounding sample packs in place of real instruments. Finally, the composition makes liberal use of "leitmotifs", or repeating themes for various characters and concepts. It's a common and well-understood technique, but here it also means that the music gets repetitive very quickly. The short looping tracks and generic sample sets also add to the repetitiveness.
The characters are all memorable, but they're also all kind of plain. They all fit common stereotypes or tropes. Their personalities are all fairly one-dimensional. The choices they make are all predictable and of no consequence to you, nor can the player really influence the way they live their life.
So, a note about the story. Lots of people I'm sure will claim that this game is one where your choices matter, but it's not as cool as it sounds. Basically, the game has three endings: a "good" ending, an "evil" ending, and a "neutral" ending. The "good" and "evil" endings only happen if you make *all* of your choices one way or the other, and the "neutral" ending happens in any other case (I'm skipping over a detail here about how the neutral and good endings work together, but my point remains). That kind of "decision-making" is absolutely ham-fisted and not any better than the silly "morality" systems you'll see other, bigger RPGs do. No choices you make in the "neutral" ending really affect how other characters live their lives or judge you, there aren't any morally ambiguous choices anywhere, and you have no leeway in the other endings to make them your own (well, ok, there are some dialog options you can make, but they have no effect on the story).
One huge aspect of the game that absolutely adds to its charm is how it plays off and makes fun of common video game elements and tropes. Anybody who's played many games will see the significance of avoiding violence. Anybody who's played an oldschool RPG will get the grinding. Anybody who's opened a Word document will shiver when a character mentions your save file. But it also takes some wrong steps. The game showing you that you're allowed to "save" your game and "continue" from an earlier point, before mocking you for trying again, is cute, but it also absolutely violates the trust it has with the player. I almost gave up playing entirely when that happened to me for the first time early in the game. Yet, it doesn't go all the way either. The self-proclaimed creator called it a "niche RPG", and that adds to in-game evidence that this game was originally meant for a very specific audience - those that have played many classic RPGs, possibly specifically in an emulator. That part of the game is not going to resonate or have its full effect with very many players, but at the same time, it doesn't actually have much significance except for a few scenes and story options.
(ok, rant over, begin the gushing)
But man oh man if this isn't still an incredible piece of work! Like, the characters are stereotypical, but they all have an interesting backstory. The backstories are always only hinted at in dialog, except for maybe one or two flashback sequences, so you kind of have to piece together what happened before your character arrived, and figure out everybody's relationship to eachother. More, the most interesting details are only ever expanded on in the "evil" storyline, because the characters are in such a radically different situation. The "moral compass" system is broken, but it still really works! And you really do get to know all of the characters - by the end you will not only have had significant hang-out time with the coolest of folks, but you will have met and gotten to know the life stories of every random-encounter enemy (and each one has a dream and a future, which is revealed in the credits - how cute is that!). It's certainly a testament to the work that there is *so much* good fan art out there. I'm sure you've seen some of it. So cool! There's also a bunch of "hidden" extra stuff that is hard to get to unless you look deep into the game, which reveals a secret backstory, and is exactly how I'd want to do hidden stuff in a game if I ever did that. And then, jeez, there's that one character (you'll know who I'm talking about) - he only has like 10 minutes of screen time, but it's written well enough and has enough supporting backstory that I, and so many others, just... just love him so much. The overall plot is kind of drawn out and contrived, and really only exists to support the characters, but it's still great, it's still filled with cross-connections, and it's probably the most beautifully tragic story I've ever heard. When people say they cried when they played this game, it's no joke. Tears of joy and sorrow - they're both there. After I finished playing I went and watched a Let's Play, and when they got to a room that referenced the end of the game (the LPers totally oblivious of course), I wept for the first time since I was a child. That's some good writing (and composing).
Anyway - highly recommended. Play the game, play it twice if you want, share it with your friends, your family (it's actually pretty kid-safe. It deals with some dark themes, but there's only one swear, one tobacco reference, one alcohol reference, and one depiction of blood - all skippable, and nothing more "mature" than that), watch some LPs, partake in the fandom. Most of all, have fun - and don't have a bad time.

One of my favorite games of all times, I have been playing this game for almost a year now, and while I have not played for all that long I have still seen the good and bad, the beauty and the horror, although facepunch has done some things that a lot of people dislike, they still do thier best to make it fun for everyone.
This game has it's disadvantages, and with every wipe something new comes up, wether it is a glitch, or an unfair balance. But I have notice one thing that always comes up, solo players get nerfed plenty of times. There are many ways that Garry could do to fix this, but with every fix comes a disadvantage. For example, if they added a new gun, or even buffed a weapon that noobs (or fresh wipes) can easily make, that would make it to where noobs could easily reck the top tier players, this was a thing at a time, with crossbows, and stone spears (before the slight nerf) it was too easy to gang bang fully geard players.
This game is always getting updates, and fixes. Every thursday they come out with a new (usually big) update, this is good since a lot of games thier creators give up on a game, wether it is because they are making a new game, or if they just do not care for it anymore. Although this game may still be in early access it is still a wonderful game, and i would say that is most definetely worth the $20.00 US that it costs.
Personaly I think that they work on things that do not really need to be fixed, or at least not at the moment. For example, the bears, oh god the bears, first of all thier AI is unbelievably screwed, they will get you throu walls, and they will climb a mountain in seconds. This is something that every player agrees needs to be fixed, But i think that Garry just wants people to get killed or exposed out of nowhere, example - if you are going out in a group to raid or something, and you are trying to sneak and a bear comes up on you, you are forced to use your gun if you have one, now you can come prepared for this situation by carrying a BP with some wood, or bring a silenced weapon. However most people don't wanna bring a silencer since it screws the gun, and most of the time you are almost dead by the time you can build a foundation to be protected from the bear, or even building blocked. Doggo's however are easily killed if you have a bow or even a hatchet, so with wolfs you can take the little dmg they deal in the time it takes to kill them with a mele or bow type weapon.
That is some of my thoughts on rust, and if you are having doubnts of buying the game, well throw those in the trash and buy the game, it is worth every penny it costs.

Ok here goes my 100% review of DayZ Standalone Early Access.  This game is about you and how you can survive there is no right way to play this game, you can be a salesman on the coast, a scary psycho clown that kills and tortures people, a survivor who lives of the land that hunts and fish, theres a billion different playstlyes you can use to play with.   The map size is 225 squared Kilometers and is always getting bigger with every patch and more interesting.  The game never ever plays out the same it can be one of the most rewarding experiences when you get to meet and teamup with fellow survivors and become life long friends, i've met 5 people that I play with almost every day in DayZ Standalone.  Theres just so much content in this game that people dont explore or use its mindblowing.  I have 1,400 hours in this game and I have yet to say to myself how I regret this purchase.  BUT this game is not perfect it still has lots of problems the game is far from finished it still has a host of things yet to be added to the game.  So the reason I have 100% faith in this game getting finished is the Dev Team they are proabably the most underrated game developers I have every heard about they are working and slaving over this game and they have so much passion for this game, if only all of you where watching there Twitter feed and read there status reports off there website
you would know that Dev team cares more than any of us.  I have been playing the Experimental branch (0.61 EXP) for the past 3 weeks and I haven't seem them release so many hotfixes and patches before, every single day they have come out with a patch to fix or add atleast 2 things.  Every one is talking about how this game is taking 3 years to develop blah blah blah its for GOOD REASON its not just because there slow or dont care its because they keep deciding to add more things to make this the greatest game it can be they are practically remaking the whole flippin game by completly remaking a new game enigine which came with the latest stable patch (0.60) which improved everything from FPS to how the game looks, they just added a new sound engine to the experimentla branch and I have never heard of more realistic gunshots and animal noises.  They are redoing a new player controller to make the game way more smooth and realistic.  But if you havent sunk  1400 hours like me and my friends and than you have only touched the tip of the iceberg because theres so much I have yet to explore or find or do.  If you are on the fence of making this purchase for this game please do some more research and watch some youtube and twitch streams.  So see you all in Chernarus!

Drawing inspirations from the classical Earthbound series, this game shines a bright light upon those recreations and leaves a canvas for many more additions that make this game unique and memorable in it's own style.
Undertale features a genderless and mysterious child who delves into the underworld beneath the land of Humans, where monsters live. Naturally, this tests the gamer and leads a perception of "monsters" to not all be chaotic or evil! This game truly is a game of choice, with many possible endings and even more memorable characters, events and lines of dialogue that'll leave you in tears, laughing or otherwise.
As I do recommend this game to any gamer who holds a strong love for Earthbound or any generic RPG, i do NOT recommend doing research on this game beforehand as the best experience comes from your first impressions and decisions based on the world you find yourself suddenly in! Good luck out there, and remember.

This game has it's disadvantages, and with every wipe something new comes up, wether it is a glitch, or an unfair balance. But I have notice one thing that always comes up, solo players get nerfed plenty of times. There are many ways that Garry could do to fix this, but with every fix comes a disadvantage. For example, if they added a new gun, or even buffed a weapon that noobs (or fresh wipes) can easily make, that would make it to where noobs could easily reck the top tier players, this was a thing at a time, with crossbows, and stone spears (before the slight nerf) it was too easy to gang bang fully geard players.
This game is always getting updates, and fixes. Every thursday they come out with a new (usually big) update, this is good since a lot of games thier creators give up on a game, wether it is because they are making a new game, or if they just do not care for it anymore. Although this game may still be in early access it is still a wonderful game, and i would say that is most definetely worth the $20.00 US that it costs.
Personaly I think that they work on things that do not really need to be fixed, or at least not at the moment. For example, the bears, oh god the bears, first of all thier AI is unbelievably screwed, they will get you throu walls, and they will climb a mountain in seconds. This is something that every player agrees needs to be fixed, But i think that Garry just wants people to get killed or exposed out of nowhere, example - if you are going out in a group to raid or something, and you are trying to sneak and a bear comes up on you, you are forced to use your gun if you have one, now you can come prepared for this situation by carrying a BP with some wood, or bring a silenced weapon. However most people don't wanna bring a silencer since it screws the gun, and most of the time you are almost dead by the time you can build a foundation to be protected from the bear, or even building blocked. Doggo's however are easily killed if you have a bow or even a hatchet, so with wolfs you can take the little dmg they deal in the time it takes to kill them with a mele or bow type weapon.
That is some of my thoughts on rust, and if you are having doubnts of buying the game, well throw those in the trash and buy the game, it is worth every penny it costs.

Where to start DayZ?  It's an idea so good that it spawned a flood of copycat games rushed to market to gain a quick easy buck, it's also a very controversial title due to it's "long" development cycle.  Many people despise DayZ for this, however, I believe it is severely misunderstood.  Yes, the game has been in development for longer than anticipated, no this is not uncommon for software development, especially when goals change, and it is decided to basically rebuild the engine out from under the game.  And no, the developers have not abandoned the title, a company this big couldn't get away with something like that without killing its credibility and possibility of profits later.  The game's been significantly reworked so far, with a new renderer (immensely improved performance), sound engine (beautiful sounds everywhere), and player controller (basically changes everything about how you do anything) coming sometime soon, and beta seemingly just around the corner, DayZ's looking a whole lot better now than it ever has before.
This is why this type of early access should not exist.

This game is awesome! A unique comic-book-style world with lots of colorful characters, crazy wildlife, sarcasm and satire, action skills, epic loot, crazy weapons, and plenty of opportunities to use them in over-the-top ways. I felt immersed in the imaginative (and fairly expansive) world and my character(s), and finding a good, rare, or legendary item continues to excite.
Overall, I definitely recommend it. Like any game, though, it's not without its flaws. I found the hard limits on backpack and bank size (even after all upgrades) to be much too strict, leaving me to have to spend lots of time managing my inventory - something that the game devs ironically said they were trying to avoid by imposing the limits in the first place. This was by far the biggest issue for me.
Also at times during the campaign I found myself stuck without ammo due to several spots with multiple bosses in a row and no chance to properly load up on ammo. Finally, sometimes if I had to backtrack a bit, bosses that I already took major effort to kill would sometimes respawn so that I had to kill them again. These issues are fairly minor in the scheme of things.
After I got tired of always running out of backpack space and the hassle of maintaining loot mules, I quit the game for a while. I recently discovered a method that kinda sorta lets me fit more loot, and I am back to enjoying the brilliance of the rest of the game. Maybe future Borderlands successors will address this issue.

Many people below have discussed the community as being the defining negative factor of Rust. However, I think this is what sets Rust apart from other survival games in that the gameplay is much more based around Survival of the Fittest.
Rust is an excellent survival game when it comes to content and usability. Some weapons are glitchy, and there hasn't been as great a focus on improving base design as there has been in on adding weapons and tools, but it is still a great game.
The "kill on sight" characteristic of the community is not a result of toxic players, it is a result of how the game is designed. The end goal for nearly every player is to gain enough resources to make C4 and rockets to raid other people. Killing fresh spawns comes from this, as you can steal resources from players who may be trying to build their own base. Keep in mind, these fresh spawns will eventually become the players who kill on sight as well.
Rust also has a slight learning curve that people tend to ignore before writing a negative review. Often times, fresh spawns start out mining without sourcing any way to defend themselves. That is how fresh spawns get killed. By crafting items such as a bow or even a hatchet, you have an edge over any fresh spawn and can even take down a geared player with a gun. Crafting a bow is not out of reach of a fresh spawn either; less than 5 minutes of gathering will provide you with enough resources to craft one.
To thoroughly enjoy this game, which I do, you have to accept the fact that Rust's gameplay is designed for players to benefit from murdering and stealing from other players. You may come across people who want to base with you, but that only lasts for so long. In the end, Rust is a game of betrayal just as much as it is a game of survival.

Before I start, let me just say, I enjoy Rust, but I write reviews to help people decide whether they will invest their money in a game or not. I will list the pros and cons, with a nuetral approach (as nuetral as I can get). With that said, here is the review:
Rust is a great game with barely any bugs/glitches. The main "issue" is the playerbase. Most people who play Rust will only befriend you when you are fresh spawns, and 75% of the time, they will betray you later on. If you find yourself in a situation where you are a fresh spawn, and they other person had a gun, they will shoot you because they like wasting bullets for rocks and a torch. Also, 50% of the fresh spawns that you will encounter that won't betray you later on, are the ones that charge at you with a rock without saying anything.
Aside from SoS PvP, there is your base. If you don't want to get raided, you must spend the first 3 hours collecting supplies so you can get 1 layer of honeycombing so you don't get raided, and don't even think about using a standard key lock, because if you forget to make a spare and don't have 100 wood lying around, when you die you are trapped in your base with no key to unlock your door and escape your own home. On your first day of Rust, you will be excited if you made a base. If you did your research on base building, you might have a nice home to come back to the next day. If you did not do your research, chances are you left the game with your base made of twigs, which can get knocked down in 5 swings from a stone hatchet.
In conclusion, you won't have a problem with rust if you are patient enough to get supplies before interacting with other players, or you could take a chance at befriending a freshie, and maybe he won't betray you!

I've been a player of Rust since the game first came out. I remember Legacy and all of it's bugs and memories and great moments. I really did enjoy Rust for its simplicity and how I could get together with a few friends and have some fun. When I first heard of them restarting Rust entirely and changing the interface, I was rather upset and stuck with Legacy until the new Rust was relatively stable.
Honestly, the New Rust is definitely a step above Legacy. A lot of people complain about how the maps are too large, or how the community is extrememly toxic and KOS (kill on sight). Although those both may be true, it gets rid of a huge problem that many players were angry with; being killed upon spawn.
The old map was very small, only about 25% of it was actually inhabitited by players or was a decent spot for players to settle, anywhere else would take you days to actually expand upon. Because of this, many new people couldn't really get out of the naked stage unless you had a group of friends with you. If you did have a group of friends, it maybe took you guys a few hours until you had everything useful, and then you too found yourself killing nakeds. This gave rust a really bad reputation and little playability.
With the new expansion of map generation (not just the same old rust map), addition of many differents weapons and items, and increase in graphics. The game was reborn with a lot more depth, replaybility, and immersion.
I have read some reviews claiming that you can't get anywhere by yourself in the new game. This honestly depends on what kind of server you join (in which there are loads). If you join a server with almost 100 people on it... Yes, you are going to die often, especially alone, expect that. But say you join a server with about 30-40 people on it. That is where the game is loads of fun. Just enough people to pose a threat, but not a ton to where you see campfires and people every  10 meters.
I myself have been able to solo in a server with an average of 50 people, it may be a challenege, but is definitely not impossible. With the new randomly generated maps, there are numerous viable spots to build a base at that not everyone on the server will know of.
If you are a new player or thinking about buying the game. Each rust review is going to be different. Some are negative because they got rid of the old Rust, some because they don't like the Kill on Sight community. But these all depend on how the players play the game, and reflects pretty well on that. This is a very good game in and of itself and its only going to continue getting better. You just have to be the one to make what you want out of it.
