In a gaming market overflowing with brooding, dark, serious shooters and RPGs, a game like Borderlands 2 is a breath of fresh air.
This game is fun and funny, a great combination. The characters are wonderfully unique, and the dialogue makes me chuckle all the time. The gameplay is very much centered around the loot: guns, guns, and more guns. There are TONS of weapons to choose from, with 5 different classes including Assualt Rifles, SMGs, Snipers, Shotguns, and Launchers. You'll get them by completeing quests or looting crates and bodies, both of which you fill find a lot of.
I do have some mechanics issues...driving doesn't always feel smooth to me and can be annoying. The enemy AI is often bafflingly bad, specifically when they seemed to lose awareness of you if you step back a few feet. Even when I have a clear sight line to an enemy, they will leave combat mdoe and return to patrolling. Once I had a gun pinned behind cover, and after a few seconds he just stood straight up and started casually walking away, saying something like "you better run!". Finally, the save system is terrible. There are no manual saves that I'm aware of, and quiting mid play will often send you back several checkpoints. This can be very frustrating.
Despite those small flaws the game is loads of fun to play, and I've enjoyed every hour so far. If you like shooters and RPGs, this is for you!

I am a huge fan of full loot pvp. I grew up playing Wurm Online, and though I came to find that game pay-to-win as I got older (and I eventually got banned from that game for complaining about it), there is nothing like that feeling of your heart racing in an intense pvp situation. I dearly miss that feeling. The first time I had that feeling, I thought I was having a heart attack. But eventually, I got more used to it. And it helped me to evolve and become a stronger person. Its like the thrill of riding a roller coaster. Its unpleasant, but strangley addicting and enjoyable because of how intense it is. PvP can be an ultimate test of your cognative ability, and with full loot involved, it also is a huge test of your emotional control, especially when your on the losing side. This is something that, for younger people, can be very overwelming at times. I've even seen fully grown adults rage after losing something in full loot, simply due to the investment involved in getting what they lost.
That said, Rust has these things. I missed PvP dearly, so when I found rust I jumped on it. I first played in a small gaming community with a bunch of friends. We built a base, and some other people in the community built an opposing base, and we fought back and forth. We made deals to never raid when offline, and the game was a lot of fun and action. Several newer kids to the genre of full loot had to learn the ropes, and I was glad to teach them how to have fun despite the intense drama of the situation. We had a lot of fun, until we found out that an admin, who happened to be in the opposing clan on the server, was spawning in thousands of high ql metals and building a massive base. Then he raided our base when we were offline, and said someone else did it. So all 12 of us left the server, and my fun times in rust ended.
After these events, our little group split tried to find a new community. Sadly, everywhere we went, everyone was hostile. We found that our situation on our community server was a special one, and that the vast majority of the rust community will KOS you without even talking. The game was no longer a game about teamwork, negotiation, and conversation. It became a game of trying not to be killed by ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s who wont even laugh when you make a joke after walking up to them. So pretty much everyone in our little group left and stopped playing the game at this point.
Now, I understand that PvP is meant to be hostile, and it attracts all sorts of nasty individuals who want to get their "fix" of being a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. This isn't a bad thing, it makes the game more interesting. Even I like playing as the badguy in pvp games (thought I make it clear that out of character, I'm friendly with everyone because its just a game). The problem isn't that these individuals are in the community, the problem in my opinion is that there is NO BREAK from the action. There is no in between time between time where you can cool down, unless you find a special community like we had before (which is very rare). This is very different from Wurm, because in the land of your kingdom, you could make friends easily. There is a sense of patriotism for your kingdom, a sense of loyalty to your comrades. This is something a PvP game needs deerly in my opinion, and its the only thing keeping it from becoming a call of duty style death match. There needs to be other groups other than the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s who want to kos you. There needs to be some nice people mixed in, to keep things from becoming bland. In rust, unless you get invited into some gaming clan, your screwed from the get go. Noone will talk with you. If you are super lucky, you might find someone willing to talk, but this is rare because these sorts of people don't play this game.
TL;DR This game is bad, because there is literally no break from the intensity of full loot PvP. There is little politics other than one guy is stronger than another so he will kill him without mercy. This makes it a bland game that is nothing more than a deathmatch, which is ok but not what I'm looking for in a full loot pvp game.

Everyone shoots on sight, which makes sense if you're killing potential rivals or threats, but that rule of engagement applies to people that just spawned too. Unless you know people on your server of choice, or you luck out and no one kills you while you get the remaining resources that weren't stockpiled, you WILL have a bad time.
$20 for a "survival" game that at its core is so ♥♥♥♥ing simple is ridiculous. I would rather play the Stranded mod for Garry's Mod. It's that bad and the game is simple enough to make that comparison.
I will never recommend this game. It's a game with a barrier to entry, even after paying. There is no incentive for buying this game because you will struggle to just PLAY the game, and if you survive past that, you'll enjoy the very limited crafting/build options.

First review ever here.
I really began playing this game in October 2016 and i'm writing this in late December.
I love and hate this game.
I still recommend it.
Many reviews here mentionned the community. Yes, the community is a pain. Mainly because, like others have said, of the killing on sight and the constant raiding, on and offline.
KoS  in itself isn't a problem: a lot of people enjoy it and it's their right.
I don't.
It's not the way I want to play Rust. The problem comes when you realize that if you want to play, solo or in a clan, on a high pop server, it's almost mandatory for you to take the KoS approach. Raiding may be a bit different in that regard and that aspect is kind of at the base of the game.
This is where I am right now: I want to play with the risk involved, which is real and thrilling, in trying to build something on a high pop server because, obviously, there is people there. But you keep having to start again and again, especially if you don't KoS.
Then, you get tired of that and you go to a lower pop server and it's good, for a time, because you can build something, but nobody cares, yourself included, and you then wonder what to do. So you go back to that high pop server and the cycle keeps going.
I would really love that the devs, if it's in their intentions, implement a system that permits KoS and raiding as a way of playing, but also encourages something deeper that would make building a community or any other type of playing a more common practice.
Rust could be much more than a stronghold-defense-'til-the-next-wipe and a murder-to-the-top kind of a game. I don't know if it will become more than that or if the community itself could provoke the change. As of now, tough, it is enjoyable for what it is, but deeply frustrating at the same time. Being that way, I had my fun with it, but it'll lose a player like me sooner than later.

Others have written reviews dissing this game for its fandom, anyone curious about this game and its quality should disregard those reviews, as the "bad fandom" does not reflect if this game is good or not. To cut to the point, this game is good. Great, actually.
-Soundtrack: The soundtrack is good, as the tags suggest; very catchy songs. I find myself humming them all the time.
-Humor: Very funny jokes, the good type of bad puns.
-Plot: The story, on the surface, is okay; but farther into the game you learn about its backstory, which is very good. The game also leaves some unsolved lore mysteries for its dedicated fans to discover and solve.
-Gameplay: The active battle system is one of the most unique I've seen in an RPG. Certain aspects of the battle system change occasionally to make things more interesting; namely, the way the player can dodge attacks. Battles also have mechanics unheard of in the genre, such as the ability to interact with the opponent, as well as being able to grant your opponent mercy.
-Ending (spoiler free, don't worry!): The ending varies depending on how you play, mostly depending on actions you take in battles. All 3 core endings are good in their own ways. UnderTale is a game best experienced with know knowledge of it when going in.
-To Wrap it All Up, UnderTale is a great game with a few minor flaws at most, I would definitely recommend to anyone.

Others have written reviews dissing this game for its fandom, anyone curious about this game and its quality should disregard those reviews, as the "bad fandom" does not reflect if this game is good or not. To cut to the point, this game is good. Great, actually.
-Soundtrack: The soundtrack is good, as the tags suggest; very catchy songs. I find myself humming them all the time.
-Humor: Very funny jokes, the good type of bad puns.
-Plot: The story, on the surface, is okay; but farther into the game you learn about its backstory, which is very good. The game also leaves some unsolved lore mysteries for its dedicated fans to discover and solve.
-Gameplay: The active battle system is one of the most unique I've seen in an RPG. Certain aspects of the battle system change occasionally to make things more interesting; namely, the way the player can dodge attacks. Battles also have mechanics unheard of in the genre, such as the ability to interact with the opponent, as well as being able to grant your opponent mercy.
-Ending (spoiler free, don't worry!): The ending varies depending on how you play, mostly depending on actions you take in battles. All 3 core endings are good in their own ways. UnderTale is a game best experienced with know knowledge of it when going in.
-To Wrap it All Up, UnderTale is a great game with a few minor flaws at most, I would definitely recommend to anyone.

I enjoy this game very much.
I'd say it's a refreshing change of pace from the typical 2.5d Action RPGs like Torchlight 2, PoE, and Diablo 3.
While some of the traditional elements like Hardcore are missing, the same awesome sense of progression and loot whoring still exists on the crazy planet of Pandora. With 6 possible character classes to choose from, each with it's own variety of builds and playstyles to suit almost any Action RPG fan.
Gun play is satisfying and it's enjoyable to mow down enemies using your abilities or that kickass gun you just found in a chest.
Borderlands really shines in its excellent writing. Characters have their own distinct personality and it's enjoyable to listen to the many quips and comments they make.
As for cons, the loot system in this game isn't as good or have as much variety of Borderlands 1.
If you want to be a hardcore Vault Hunter then you will realize that past a certain point all of those flashy purple rarity weapons will pale in comparison to legendaries.
The endgame of Borderlands 2 almost shoehorns you into using certain legendaries or uniques which feels restrictive. Even character builds also suffer somewhat from this problem, where you'll find certain character trees useless in the endgame, such as Salvadors Brawn tree.
Farming for gear can also be a chore as top gear usually drops from raid bosses instead of farming from levels and dungeons like in PoE, Torchlight 2, or Diablo 3.
Conclusion:
While this game is a fun and enjoyable experience, the endgame feels restrictive in build variety. Sure you'll survive but the min maxing "problem" (some can see min maxing as something to reach for) is iffy.
I give this game a 8.5/10. Would definitely recommend for a fun co op and solo experience.

One of the better survival games I've played.  Survival games are one of the largest attractions to PC gaming, or at least that's the case for myself.  Rust and Ark: Survival Evolved are two of the largest survival and crafting/resource games in the market.  For myself, I find Rust to be far superior due to it's harsher mechanics and unforgiving gameplay.  That being said, if you like that kind of thing then fantastic, this game will probably be your fancy.  However, if you find dying and losing all of your inventory and progress a game-killer, then this isn't your choice.
Pros:
Rust is by far the most visually attractive survival games, there are moments this game looks comparable to AAA titles.
The hardcore aspect of Rust is fantastic, real nudity, inabiliy to choose your race and gender, and hunger and thirst make this game feel pretty difficult and real at times.
The game can be very rewarding, when you get your first shotgun or rifle and start killing players and animals, things get crazy and amazingly awesome.  That being said, this can all be taken away by unfriendly players, bad luck, or poor decision making.
With some friends or without, the game's openness and possibility leaves a lot of room for unforgettable moments and fun times to be had.
Cons:
The game can be fairly difficult to understand at first, learning how to build, reinforce, craft and customize can take frustrating hours, especially when it's so easy to be set back hours or days because of the ignorance of the game.
When you get raided or die, it's seriously not fun and can ruin the game for a couple days.  While I would say that we should all just accept that it's part of the game, however, it is unbelievably aggravating.
Resources in the game are fairly hard to find in mass amount, this is good to promote player interacting and need to survive, however it can feel unfair and cheap if you spend hours wandering the radius of your base and end up still not finding anything in mass, whether that's wood or stone or animals.
Giant bases are intense and daunting for a new player, they look cool, make you wonder what you could end up being, and make you cautious.  However, with giant bases comes lots of players, and it's not uncommon for these bases to decide to leave and mess up everyone's day nearby.  Very very upsetting.
The cons list is full, however this is a survival game, if you can enjoy the cons and love the pros, then Rust will give you a great time.  However if the unforgiving nature or potential to be reduced to step 0 at any moment seems too angering to bear, then best to walk away from this.

This game is so "badass" you don't even know the extend of that word until you play it. Now I am not gonna tell what content this game has (areas' weapons, classes, missions, etc.) because you can read that anywhere. No I am gonna tell you why this game is worth owning.
Borderlands 2 can be desribed as a hybrid between Fallout, Team Fortress 2, Diablo, and other RPG's and FPS's. It takes just but anything from good from these series and put it into the game. The game has a comic style graphics which makes it unique and different to look at instead of all these fotorealistic games. The gameplay is typical FPS gameplay, with those things that follow so people will quickly find that familiar. The RPG elements are also farily simple and remind you of other RPG's (you level up your character, use skill points on various skills and equip weapons and and stuff acording to your current lvl). You accept quests from people and there are a ton of side quests as well as the main story quests.
So all these things sound familiar, so what exactly sets this game apart from the rest? Well, aside from the graphics style, its gotta be the story! The characters! The humor! Every character in the game (be it NPC's or your character) are very well done, have their own personality, they are memorable and perfectly voice acted. This game takes itself seriously enough to that extend that's okay to throw in some well placed humor. Trust me, the main villian in the game is a guy who you just love to hate. He's that well created, personality-wise. Also your allies like Claptrap (my favorite) and a girl called Tiny Tina are all very unique characters and when they got something to say, you just listen.
The game takes around a good solid 15-20 hours to complete (more if you do all the side quests) and takes even double the time to get all the way to max lvl (50 without those upgrade packs). With the season pass which includes the 4 main DLC packs, you can expect to spend around 80 hours to complete them all (all side quests included) and after that, there is end game content like raid bosses and stuff. So all round, you get your moneys worth when you buy this game, be it the normal edition or the GOTY edition that I bought. This game doesn't choose between quantity or quality, it delivers both! And the game has 4 player co-op, so you can play through all the content with up to 3 buddies.
The game also has a few bugs and glitches. Ex there is texture loading every time you enter a new area. Enemies may clip through certain terrain. You may get stuck somewhere (especially between rocks) if you are too eager and there is no unstuck command so you have to commit suicide to respawn at a checkpoint station. Oh and a friendly advice: When someone speaks to you through the intercom (their name and picture will appear in the upper right corner) stop up and listen. There is a chance that when moving through a certain area it may trigger a dialouge and it will overdub any current dialouge you may have. It means that when a npc is speaking to you or just speaking in general through the intercom and you keep moving, you may trigger another npc to start talking and the previous npc who was talking will stop and it won't come back. Because of this, you may miss important mission information, story information, a good joke or humor that will be lost. So I advice you to stop and listen when someone speaks. Other than what I have mentioned, there is nothing else. No gamebreaking bugs or anything.
So for the final rating, I will give this game a 9/10, simply because I don't think the game is "perfect", there is certainly room for improvement, but it is on its way. Go out and buy this game now, it's too badass to ignore :-D
Why is there even a question? It's like asking, "Why is there beauty in the universe?". You just accept it and bask in its wondrousness!

WARNING: THIS REVIEW GIVES MINOR SPOILERS FOR UNDERTALE. VIEW AT YOUR OWN DISCRETION
Throughout this single year that it's been out, Undertale has been yanked in and out of these two sides of love and hate across the internet. The ones who love it praise it for using a bullet-hell battle system that encourages pacifist playthroughs and telling a humorous and emotional 7-hour thrill ride. On the other hand, the ones who aren't very fond of Undertale criticize it for its obsessive fanbase that creates these weird fan drawings and constantly pushes people to play the game, even if they might not want to.
As you can see, each side has their own reason for liking or hating the game. Yet, despite this, regardless of whether or not you enjoy Undertale, this experience isn't mainly about doing either of these things at all. It's about conversing with a joyous and friendly flower, only to freak out when he reveals that he's a total sicco that wants to murder you and everything that breathes. It's about feeling uneasy knowing that you have to do a randomly generated puzzle, only to laugh when it was just going to generate a straight path instead. It's about having a sense of insecurity when an over-achieving skeleton asks you to hang out with him in his room. It almost seems like he's going to try and "make a move" on you, but he really just makes a humorous scene where he just gives you spaghetti that he made as a gift. It's about encouraging a nervous knight to confess his feelings to his armorless and buff friend, only to be weirded out when you realize the two knights are gay for eachother. Most importantly, though, it's about making you feel like the biggest jerk ever for the times you killed a monster or two, even if you thought you had no choice.
The main purpose for Undertale is to make you feel uncomfortable. Yes, the game can make you cry. Yes, it has a genius combat system in a genre dominated by games that play things safely. However, all of this adds up to take you out of your comfort zone. Undertale puts you in situations where you're interacting with people you don't really like or just have a lifestyle you might not agree with. At first, I thought Papyrus was just some narcissistic dork, but he's really just someone who pursues his goals with a fiery passion. He just shows it in a way normal people wouldn't understand. When I first saw Undyne in her ominous armor, I thought she was just some sociopathic knight who was just trying to kill me out of pure evil. When I fought her, however, I found out that she's really just an extremely passionate fish who was only trying to kill me for the sake of the people that she defends. And when I was about to meet Alphys, I pictured her being this old and wise scientist that knew everything. Instead, though, she's this socially-awkward otaku that is so obsessed with anime that she "confirms" that anime is a real-life record of human history to the monsters of her home. She also suffers from a lack of self-confidence in herself, and constantly tries her best to be all she can be by posting statuses constantly on her social media page and trying to date Undyne.
The whole game does all of this, these encounters with the strange and the twist on gameplay, to make you realize that in the real world, not everything is as it seems. Not everybody is this invincible being that people like to stage themselves as. Not everybody is what you perceive them to be. The dorks, the muslims, and even the smart kids at your school are not what people tend to generalize them as being. They're regular, normal people like you and me. They're truly real individuals that have a heart and that have short-comings just like everyone else, and the game conveys this message perfectly through its determination to make you understand people and situations that would otherwise make you nervous to remind you to just love people and not to over-think things in life. It is a constant cell-phone reminder that people should never, EVER forget to do one thing:
To love.
So, yes, I do recommend this masterpiece. Though, not just because I think it's one of the greatest games of all time or because it is an emotional thrill ride. Rather, I believe that, if you're open about it, Undertale can cause you to look at life differently and maybe even change you entirely for the better. Yes, I know I might sound like an auction man running his mouth to try and get a product off his hands, and that you might be thinking that this is just another review that recommends a game you might not be all that into. Which is fine! I used to not be very fond of this game when I tried the free demo of it for the first time due to its old-school style, but then I played it again with an open mind, and I can now proudly say that I didn't regret a minute of playing this epic game. So, yeah, give it a go. It's one of those games you need to play before you die. You might actually think very fondly of it later on. :)

WARNING: THIS REVIEW GIVES MINOR SPOILERS FOR UNDERTALE. VIEW AT YOUR OWN DISCRETION
Throughout this single year that it's been out, Undertale has been yanked in and out of these two sides of love and hate across the internet. The ones who love it praise it for using a bullet-hell battle system that encourages pacifist playthroughs and telling a humorous and emotional 7-hour thrill ride. On the other hand, the ones who aren't very fond of Undertale criticize it for its obsessive fanbase that creates these weird fan drawings and constantly pushes people to play the game, even if they might not want to.
As you can see, each side has their own reason for liking or hating the game. Yet, despite this, regardless of whether or not you enjoy Undertale, this experience isn't mainly about doing either of these things at all. It's about conversing with a joyous and friendly flower, only to freak out when he reveals that he's a total sicco that wants to murder you and everything that breathes. It's about feeling uneasy knowing that you have to do a randomly generated puzzle, only to laugh when it was just going to generate a straight path instead. It's about having a sense of insecurity when an over-achieving skeleton asks you to hang out with him in his room. It almost seems like he's going to try and "make a move" on you, but he really just makes a humorous scene where he just gives you spaghetti that he made as a gift. It's about encouraging a nervous knight to confess his feelings to his armorless and buff friend, only to be weirded out when you realize the two knights are gay for eachother. Most importantly, though, it's about making you feel like the biggest jerk ever for the times you killed a monster or two, even if you thought you had no choice.
The main purpose for Undertale is to make you feel uncomfortable. Yes, the game can make you cry. Yes, it has a genius combat system in a genre dominated by games that play things safely. However, all of this adds up to take you out of your comfort zone. Undertale puts you in situations where you're interacting with people you don't really like or just have a lifestyle you might not agree with. At first, I thought Papyrus was just some narcissistic dork, but he's really just someone who pursues his goals with a fiery passion. He just shows it in a way normal people wouldn't understand. When I first saw Undyne in her ominous armor, I thought she was just some sociopathic knight who was just trying to kill me out of pure evil. When I fought her, however, I found out that she's really just an extremely passionate fish who was only trying to kill me for the sake of the people that she defends. And when I was about to meet Alphys, I pictured her being this old and wise scientist that knew everything. Instead, though, she's this socially-awkward otaku that is so obsessed with anime that she "confirms" that anime is a real-life record of human history to the monsters of her home. She also suffers from a lack of self-confidence in herself, and constantly tries her best to be all she can be by posting statuses constantly on her social media page and trying to date Undyne.
The whole game does all of this, these encounters with the strange and the twist on gameplay, to make you realize that in the real world, not everything is as it seems. Not everybody is this invincible being that people like to stage themselves as. Not everybody is what you perceive them to be. The dorks, the muslims, and even the smart kids at your school are not what people tend to generalize them as being. They're regular, normal people like you and me. They're truly real individuals that have a heart and that have short-comings just like everyone else, and the game conveys this message perfectly through its determination to make you understand people and situations that would otherwise make you nervous to remind you to just love people and not to over-think things in life. It is a constant cell-phone reminder that people should never, EVER forget to do one thing:
To love.
So, yes, I do recommend this masterpiece. Though, not just because I think it's one of the greatest games of all time or because it is an emotional thrill ride. Rather, I believe that, if you're open about it, Undertale can cause you to look at life differently and maybe even change you entirely for the better. Yes, I know I might sound like an auction man running his mouth to try and get a product off his hands, and that you might be thinking that this is just another review that recommends a game you might not be all that into. Which is fine! I used to not be very fond of this game when I tried the free demo of it for the first time due to its old-school style, but then I played it again with an open mind, and I can now proudly say that I didn't regret a minute of playing this epic game. So, yeah, give it a go. It's one of those games you need to play before you die. You might actually think very fondly of it later on. :)

Flawless symetry of FPS and RPG.  Great solo, better with friends. With 6 characters to play as (DLC included) and randomized loot the replayability of this game is stellar. I've logged tons of hours on my console with the family and decided on the Steam purchase and have not been disapointed.
Those that have played the original Borderlands will notice many similarities and concepts carried over.  However, the difficulty in Borderlands 2 makes it stand alone.  The hardest parts of Borderlands and now par for the course in Borderlands 2.  For this reason it's a right challenge for a straight playthrough solo.  Stopping for loot runs will make it easier, but it's still enough of a challenge to keep you interested.
The story is phenominally funny and ties in well with the original.  The cast of characters is likable and memorable, especially the show-stealing Tiny Tina.  Voice acting adds well to the game, even background characters will occasionally spout off a laugh enducing quip.
Each character is very unique in playstyle, from the brute force Salvador, to the silent but deadly Zero.  Each poses a different role in battle and has made multiple playthroughs fun for myself and family.
Gunplay has changed a lot since the original.  With the elimination of weapon proficiencies the game plays more like a traditional FPS.  I personally like the over the top advantage that they gave you, sniping with machine guns and so forth.  It leaves me feeling more like I'm in the trenches in a fight rather than playing the role of Rambo anymore, but cest la vie.
I'm definitely looking forward to future installments of the series.

Before I make it clear why I have to dislike this game so far is because of some very prominent reasons to the game. So first off like to say that the game is good, fun when you have friends, and a good sandbox mine'n'grind type of game. It has huge environments, unique variety of things to find, bases to build, things to obtain, a fantastic xp and item crafting collection and a interesting atmosphere. So all around with my friend's getting into this game we had fun experiences. Now I had no prior experience with this game when my friend's got me into it and I loved it. For the first 20 hrs or so, than realized its problems.
The reason why this game is getting my downvote is because of many elements. One thing being that the community and many of its servers are toxic and always hostile, killing one another before getting anywhere. People just waiting to raid and destroy your base, take your stuff and make you feel you have wasted time on it, and if you do die you basically lose everything you worked on, and when you leave the game you are left in your sleep whether it's from others or trolling bears, everything you obtain and took time to build can be easily lost almost just automatically. Also the Anti-Cheat does not always work for my huge metal base was raided in less than an hour or so with overpowered C4s. If you have a sleeping bag congratulations but you will still roam back to being naked and back to square one cutting down tress and trying to re-obtain your body. Second reason is that NPC/Animals clip through everything or spawn right on top of you or even sometimes literally in your base for cheap kills, that is not cool.
As I continue on my third issue with the game is that almost all servers reset and clean everything you built and accomplished back to 0 by the end of the month or following month or so. Oh you get to keep your level xp, but not your inventory stuff or the bases you built, raided or restored with your friends, and that is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. I can understand a map wipe of excess destroyed building walls and areas of course, but not the whole damn thing where you are left naked and stranded back to finding your buddies, and I find it as a huge letdown in my opinion when I first heard the news as I was really getting into it and finally learning how to build it all. Only to have it all erased? Ignorant.
Another issue is that this game is 3 years old! And still in EARLY ACCESS. Meaning it is still incomplete, unsecured and pillaged mess. When you have clipping enemies, swiped servers and no concrete established finished game is insane. Not to mention that this game that isn't finished tries to nickel and dime people with skins when it all should be officially randomized into the maps for free! These microtransaction skins aren't worth the money, and be more rewarding to find the stuff than lose it. And the developers should give those who find the stuff they search for and build a way to keep what they want even after the server wipes, and to me is unacceptable because it creates a killjoy.
Next issue with the game is it's building mechanics and deconstructions of the overall game. The building tools of areas is limited and not accurate, can have ladders and doors clipping through rock or trees and still have the issue of getting stuck. Also there is no effective demolish options for the stuff (you own and privileged) you build for your base. And because of this you will spend a colossal waste of time trying to remove the walls or doors you want to get rid of by tools or explosives, because you have to collect and create constantly to get the required amounts you need for such a project. And deep down it just is another letdown when you spend all this time trying to break into places or fix your own base on the equipment you receive only to have it all taken from you in a matter of minutes or hours by trolling raiders or players.
My final issue is the Save Mechanism. This is the big one! Ultimately if you pick a server get far in it you cannot carry any of this over to another server or save the lv you obtained. Also when you are gone, disconnected or sleeping when you save or exit the game anyone can just come and kill your guy, take their stuff and let a wolf maul you or something. Even if you have a base and a protected position you could find your guy still dead from raiders, a NPC attack, or gone a long time only to have everything swiped and erased. That is all so lowball that even your own allies can end up betraying you and stealing everything you gained. If you want type of gameplay than keep it in the PVP, not in the PVE(P) type of servers so you can keep your ♥♥♥♥. And that being said this is what kills the game in the long run, unless you are someone who has all the free time in the world to raid, pillage and plunder than be my guess but to me and the many other games I play I would have no time to really devote my life to a game like this if I am willing to never sleep again to keep up with the demand of this type of game. There are multiple routes throughout the game, but whichever route you choose, Undertale is sure to deliver. This game is definetely worth your time if you enjoyed other games like Earthbound, Final Fantasy, Legend of Zelda, and any other RPG/J-RPG.

After sinking just over 40 hours into this game, getting to know the game's ups and downs, I am writing this review.
The good: Lots of randomized guns and other loot that have stats based on "manufacturer" and "type". Loot is based around enemy levels, and the game does a good job at guiding you towards enemies that aren't too strong for you to fight. This makes for fun and addicting gameplay that moves along at a nice pace and keeps the player interested with the promise of always being able to find more powerful and more impressive loot with which you will be able to more easily dispatch the waves of baddies that you'll be required to deal with. It reminds me of the Diablo 2 formula, except they've adapted it to a first person shooter. It's a game that is very co-op focused, so if you enjoy playing with friends I would definitely recommend it.
The bad: The game is so focused on playing with friends and giving you the co-op experience they want you to have, that they practically punish anyone who plays it alone. It's almost as if they're forcing co-op down the player's throat, regardless of if they want it or not. I don't know what the intention of taking away a set percentage of the player's wallet when they die was, but it means that if you don't have a co-op buddy to revive you and make sure you don't lose that cash, you're going to lose that cash, every single time you have to respawn. The only way around this is to exploit the save and quit system by saving and quitting every time you die. This renders the mechanic of taking the player's money for dying pretty much useless. And there are still no air vehicles.
Conclusion: I would definitely have to recommend this game, but with an asterisk beside the recommendation because of the anti-single-player elements the game has.
Note to low-end PC users: This game runs at a silky smooth 30fps (60 with frequent framerate drops down to 30 in some areas if I take the framerate limit off) on my ancient Nvidia 8600 GT thanks to the magic of .ini editing, which removed most of the lighting effects and lowered all of the textures to the point where it looks like a Nintendo 64 game. If you have a low-end rig and are wondering if you can run this game, ask yourself three questions. 1) Is my card at least equivalent to a middle-end card from 2007 that only has 256mb of DDR2 video memory? 2) Do I mind if it looks like♥♥♥♥♥and runs at 640x480 resolution? 3) Do you know how to edit .ini files with notepad and use Google?
Edit: The DLC is mostly unimaginative arena-tier garbage and the devs knew it, so they made it more enticing by upping the level cap but ONLY if you purchase their boring DLC. I own a good deal of the DLC for this game and let me tell you, it's crap. Not worth it, not even for the level cap raise.

DayZ is the Marmite of gaming, you either love it or you hate it; from it's scale and realism to it's development speed and length in Alpha, people are very divided on whether it's fantastic and promising or a total scam. It's really one to make up your own opinion on.
That said, I've sunk close to 1000 hours into the Standalone (which, while content-light compared to the currently-complete mod) just feels, and looks far better, and aims to be more content rich and detailed than it's older brother. Playing a few hours while catching up with your mates about their day while jogging from Cherno to the PVP-heavy North West Airfield is a fantastic way to pass the time (again, not for everyone) and no game comes close to the sheer tension every single gunfight brings. Heart racing, brow sweating and hands shaking as you come under fire, it brings the realism of ARMA (as well as it's clunkiness, for now) and couples it with an absolute sense of fight or flight to every encounter. Run and live? Stand and fight? Take a hit and retreat?
Each scenario has it's own advantages. Survive. Get that guy's gear. Do some damage of your own before leaving. They also have their own disadvantages; nothing gained, ammo loss, health and gear.
While PVP is almost certainly guaranteed, there was more of a sense of community and cooperation in the mod. That may come, in time; but for now, DayZ stands as an excellent post-apocalyptic paranoid survior sim.
Worth a look.
And if you're on the fence, just wait until it's done. EA bugs and content void might turn you away, but the finished product will be more your cup of tea. Plenty of things to play until then!

Undertale's writing alternates between taking itself too seriously or not seriously at all. It is difficult to classify as a parody when it really wants an emotional connection. It becomes a parody when it takes the otherwise typical JRPG formula and completely, utterly upends it on a whim.
It is worth a play if you can tolerate the Earthbound-like RPG menu system and are somewhat proficient in Gradius/Galaga style "avoid collsion" games. Another requirement is probably either an understanding of what games Undertale mimics, or at least an immersion into golden-era gaming console culture.
I am finding that Undertale fits the present day situation where it is probably more entertaining to see a hardcore player streaming for others to watch, than it is to play it oneself. It also becomes a quasi "Nintendo-hard" game that requires online research for alternate endings BECAUSE there's no possible way to discover otherwise. This is opposed to something like finding Temmie Village, which is easy.
The game has a persistent state independent of beating the game (New Game+ idea). The most logical option at the end of the game dooms you to the same neutral ending again. When you've played for 16 hours in 2 or 3 days, (many people do this in Rust) you don't want to lose all the stuffed you earned from playing. In Rust you can play 12 hours a day for a week, have so many guns you are giving 5 away to everyone you meet, so many resources you have to biggest base in the server, and just have so much stuff that you worked for that you don't know what to do with. Now all of that stuff can be lost in under an hour, if people raid you. This is why people are so defensive. This is why people kill, it's part of the game. (I'm HARDCORE ranting so IDK)

I have read over reviews and all the negative ones complain about the "toxic" community. It's not as bad as they make it sound. If you get friends together or join another group/clan than you can make a base and have tons of resources and weapons. I suggest this to new players and other players who think the community is so "toxic". This is because it makes surviving "easier". It also, in my opinion, is a lot more fun to play with friends. Although, I find it fun to solo sometimes. It's fun to build a small base and not try to "have it all". It can be fun to run around with a bow every once in a while. If you are having trouble finding friends when you first buy this game, try joining a clan. Most are always accepting new members. Most servers have multiple clans that are rivals and try to raid and kill eachother, at all times. It makes it somewhat competitive and fun. When you do first join a clan, you usually are put to work by the people in charge. They make you go mine rocks and get wood. You are new to the clan and you need to earn your keep, and prove yourself. You work your way up and they trust you with weapons. You help build and grow your clan's base. You raid many many other people to help your clan flourish.
Summary: This game is IMO the best survival multiplayer game. There is so much to do and it is so fun. You gather resources, get tools, build a base, smelt ores, make guns, upgrade that base, make friends, make eniemes, raid people, get raided. When you play this game try to be nice, please don't KOS everyone. Thanks!

Undertale's writing alternates between taking itself too seriously or not seriously at all. It is difficult to classify as a parody when it really wants an emotional connection. It becomes a parody when it takes the otherwise typical JRPG formula and completely, utterly upends it on a whim.
It is worth a play if you can tolerate the Earthbound-like RPG menu system and are somewhat proficient in Gradius/Galaga style "avoid collsion" games. Another requirement is probably either an understanding of what games Undertale mimics, or at least an immersion into golden-era gaming console culture.
I am finding that Undertale fits the present day situation where it is probably more entertaining to see a hardcore player streaming for others to watch, than it is to play it oneself. It also becomes a quasi "Nintendo-hard" game that requires online research for alternate endings BECAUSE there's no possible way to discover otherwise. This is opposed to something like finding Temmie Village, which is easy.
The game has a persistent state independent of beating the game (New Game+ idea). The most logical option at the end of the game dooms you to the same neutral ending again. If one is healthy and understands the implications of the "Scorpion and the Frog" tale then how is anyone going to realize the situation more resembles the "Scorpion and the Turtle"? How does they player know that they are then supposed to choose an option *****13 TIMES***** when they have no indication in this metaphor that they are indeed a "Turtle"?
So I don't have the patience to get any other ending than my ending, where Undyne works at the hotdog stand and resents me forever for killing two moldslimes and one frog.

The thing is, Borderlands 2 is meant to have the story played through several times to unlock harder gamemodes (i.e. True Vault Hunter Mode, Ultimate Vault Hunter Mode). If you don't find having to repeat the story over a few times, you should give this game a try. To me, the thing I enjoy to do the most is hunting for the best items in the game with my friends. The grinding is real (if you choose not to ruin the fun and duplicate) but having friends will make it more enjoyable. Borderlands 2's story is packed with humor and deception, causing you to become immersed in the story as well as the gameplay. Overall, I really recommend this game if you would like to grind alongside your friends.

Oh boy, there's a lot of things I wanna say about this game.
I've thought a lot back when It first came out on Steam, I heard how everyone said the game was good and so on.
Now 1 year later, I tried it and I can't believe it. I can't believe I didn't buy this at the very beginning.
This game has such a powerful story, I can't describe it. I just love every second and minute I've spent on it.
The game is about a human child named Frisk, a girl who wakes up in the underground.
You have to explore and go through a lot of difficult situations and make decisions that will effect the game to the end.
If you like to explore and basically have something to occupy yourself with, this will be the best game for just that.
Things happen when you don't expect it, you get a view over the different characters and their life.
What's even more impressing is that the guy who made the game did all animations and sound effects by himself.
The game is not like something else you'll ever play, this is one of a kind.
I've played this game over and over many times and I still enjoy every time like the first.
I love the way you fight against monsters, there is always different ways to avoid and fight them.
The music is also one of the best things about this game, It's so great and somehow "powerful".
You'll get a different feeling from any other games.
If you happen to have some money, don't hesitate to buy this game. It's so worth the money, no doubt.
Hell yeah, that's all I have to say.

Rust is a survival game with hunger, water and health to look out for. You will be born naked in this world and youll need to survive. I would recommend to join a low populated server to start out so you dont always get killed by experience players and/or other nudes. My first reaction to the game was "par". I didnt know what to think of it because i kept dying. After a while of learning however, the Rust experience just got better and better. The graphics are excellent, I rarely run into bugs, and if you do get a bug, it doesnt actually ruin your immersive experience because the positives of the game are way up there. You'll need to survive against animals, starvation and many more obstacles. The crafting aspect of Rust is excellent as well. It's well thought of and the menus are very user friendly. The base designing is best I've seen so far. The work and imagination you can put in a base is beyond what you expect. The map size is sufficient, though a bigger map is always better. This game is everything you could want in a real apocalyptic survival game. First and foremost, it is in beta, any complaints about lag, glitches and the like are just silly because that's the whole point of a game going through alpha/beta, otherwise it would just be called released.
Second and what should be more important: gameplay. The concept is basic but great, you wake up with nothing (realistically no stat pants couldn't hurt haha) and every piece of resource you need you have to gather. One issue on some servers is that resources aren't spawning quickly enough or at all from what I hear, but that's because the game is in alpha... aside from spawning rates resource execution is great, maybe in the future they will reskin some rocks to look like discarded metal for realism, but as far as gameplay goes it's all the same. In a real survival situation you wouldn't find piles of a variety of resources naturally, just some wood and minerals. Animals are scarce in some areas and that's completely realistic too, unless you're on a farm, if there was real life apocalypse you would not see bears and boars walking around main paths constantly.
The sleeping bag is a great feature. You can save a spawn point and use a metal door to hopefully keep your things safe. This allows you to actually form alliances and make friends, but doesn't add a "haven/neutral" point in the game which makes it so much more exciting.
Lastly community discussion. Yes, the people are mean and vicious, and perhaps they are kids (I like how that's become an insult these days, it's a videogame for Christ's sake!). This is what makes this game great. Who expects there to be tons of people out there willing to help others and extend trust and a welcoming hand to total strangers in an apocalypse? Most people you run into will be desperate and selfish, some well run the other direction because they are scared, lots will become bullies because they can and a few will begin to band together in these beginning stages of hard times. This is what I've come across so far playing the game, and this is what makes it pee your pants scary...what I assume you were looking for when you bought this game.
For anyone who wants a nice community with easy to gather resources and mobs that hit you for 3% of your health, play minecraft. For those who played for 30 mins or an hour and got tired of crap server lag and crashes, and glitchy gameplay just keep in mind it's in alpha and will get better. If you don't have the patience put it on the backburner for later enjoyment!

Flawless symetry of FPS and RPG.  Great solo, better with friends. With 6 characters to play as (DLC included) and randomized loot the replayability of this game is stellar. I've logged tons of hours on my console with the family and decided on the Steam purchase and have not been disapointed.
Those that have played the original Borderlands will notice many similarities and concepts carried over.  However, the difficulty in Borderlands 2 makes it stand alone.  The hardest parts of Borderlands and now par for the course in Borderlands 2.  For this reason it's a right challenge for a straight playthrough solo.  Stopping for loot runs will make it easier, but it's still enough of a challenge to keep you interested.
The story is phenominally funny and ties in well with the original.  The cast of characters is likable and memorable, especially the show-stealing Tiny Tina.  Voice acting adds well to the game, even background characters will occasionally spout off a laugh enducing quip.
Each character is very unique in playstyle, from the brute force Salvador, to the silent but deadly Zero.  Each poses a different role in battle and has made multiple playthroughs fun for myself and family.
Gunplay has changed a lot since the original.  With the elimination of weapon proficiencies the game plays more like a traditional FPS.  I personally like the over the top advantage that they gave you, sniping with machine guns and so forth.  It leaves me feeling more like I'm in the trenches in a fight rather than playing the role of Rambo anymore, but cest la vie.
I'm definitely looking forward to future installments of the series.

My only critique would be the lack of PvE elements trying to kill you. Sure, the thudding of a bear can be terrifying if you aren't prepared to fight it, but its not enough. Players need something to be scared of other than each other so that more focus can go to the environment.
Lastly, removing visibility during the night was an interesting move, but it makes half the time spent in game almost useless without using a light source. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, but it would be nice if we could have night-vision goggles as a super rare drop/craft. Might be asking for too much, but it would certainly help.
Anyway, excellent game. 9/10. Definitely worth the money.

Borderlands 2 has a near-unlimited variety of awesome guns, which can be used on a great number of fearsome enemies.  Borderlands 2 is all about shooting the same palette-shifted enemies with the same boring weapons.  It brings the best of the Diablo-like action RPGs together with the FPS genre.  It lacks the simplicity of the former, and the skill of the latter.  The game has 4 playable classes, which can use very different playstyles.  All the classes use the same guns, so aside from their unique skill and a few passive bonuses, they all wind up playing about the same.  It has tons of secrets, easter eggs, and rewards for exploration, as well as achievements galore.  It doles out a steady drip of meaningless bonuses, based on a Big-Brother-esque monitoring of everything you do.  It has an amazing variety of environments, and some truly epic boss battles.  It parades you through spots that look spectacular, but really only offer a new sequence of boxes or chest-high walls to hide behind, and the bosses are all repetitive cycles of poking out of cover, unloading your clip, then ducking back to hide from their super attack.
It has a great story with a loathsome villain, to draw the players in.  It has a forgettable story with a cardboard-cutout villain that you're simply told to hate because of what he does off-screen, as well as his persistent audio taunts.  It has wonderful writing, with a dark comedy style that is often hilarious.  It can only muster a few cheap laughs with riffs on tired pop-culture  references and entirely predictable jokes.
Borderlands 2 is a triumph, whose huge sales figures attest to the impact it's had in the games industry.  Borderlands 2 is a trashy, manipulative, cynical appeal to the lowest common denominator, and represents everything that's wrong with modern game design.
Which is it?  Well, that depends on your perspective..

Ahh, this game. For those of you who don't like reading TL;DR : The game is fun, especially for people who like RPG's, and the Fan Base is very weird and talented.
Summary:
Undertale is a game about a small girl who climbs a mountain and trips and falls into a hole. She explores a Monster City and learns about a secret hidden past where Humans & Monsters live together. On the way she can choose wether or not she wants to kill all the Monsters, or spare and let all of them live. A fun RPG where you can play and get multiple endings, and a hidden storyline that seems to be very deep and emotional. You can make many friends, fight long and hard boss fights, and get a happy ending.
Rating:
Being an RPG it gets alot of hate from multiple people. However this game is Linear and actually extremely amazing. The game itself is (as far as i know) Completely bugless and extremely smooth. The game has a REDICULOUS amount of hidden secrets, an amazing hidden backstory along with an epic main storyline. As far as that goes, the fanbase is a bit extreme when it comes to this game, but if you ignore all of the fans, this game is really fun, very genuine, and not at all hard to beat. There are so many diffrent ways to play. You can play a: Neutral Run, Pacifist Run,  Real Pacifist Run,  No Mercy Run (Basically the same as neutral), and Geneocide Run. A Neutral run means that you can either spare or kill anyone you choose. A Pacifist Run is basically all sparing, while a Real Pacifist Run requires a bit more to it. (If you plan on Real Pacifist Run I would search up a guide.)  A No Mercy Run is whenever you meet a monster you kill it, and a genocide run means you go out of your way to kill every monster. Neutral, Pacifist, and No mercy will obtain the same ending, Real Pacifist gets another ending, And genocide gets it's own ending as well. When you buy this game your supporting a really great guy, and your getting an amazing game in return.
Final Verdict:
1 = Stay Away
5 = So-So, buy if on sale and interested
10 = Highly Recommend, buy at any price
8/10 = Highly Reccommended, buy at 20% discount or more

This game is a true amazing experience. Gameplay is well designed in which the story and side mission items are conveniently placed. There are no questions about smooth gameplay and characters with personalities and great introductions to them. This is not another shoot 'em up game, you actually have to make up your strategy along the way and change it according to gameplay differences with each character you choose and enemies you face.
Pros:
+art style
+gameplay design through missions
+characters have personalities
+convenient item placement
Cons:
-robotic and stiff enemy movement
-a lot of invisible walls
DETAILS:
You don't get rewarded for your shooting skill. Let's take a sniper for example. If you want to use a sniper in combination with your character you need to find your enemy's weak spots, and by doing so, you have more chance to survive sparing some ammo. Now, that works for a little while you're around 10-20 lvl. Later the enemies are strong even in their weak spots, and this makes you vulnerable. It doesn't matter if you have a stronger sniper than before. You start to lose ammo and take other guns instead. Now you need to get closer to your enemy because you don't have any progress with sniper. You notice that one weapon doesn't do enough damage to all your enemies (usually in the number of 5-10 and above). You notice that you're low on health and your shield isn't recharging fast enough. This makes you to get to ''fight for your life'' mode and gain some of the health and full shield which beats the purpose of the game. There really shouldn't be flaws like this that gamers exploit.
Besides the game changing flaw, I should really talk about item placement. As I said before, items with which you need to interact or pick are conveniently placed according to storyline. There's one mission in which you need to deliver some packages on time to mailboxes near the shore. Now, in any other game the items would be placed in same distances from another and would waste your time in which the time is of importance. In this game, mailboxes are conveniently placed as they would be in real life, but now time isn't that much important as your ability to get through enemies and find all placed mailboxes (some good designing♥♥♥♥♥♥right there).
The last concern of mine are invisible walls, true enemies of every gamer. Now, this includes the fact that you have to stand exactly in front of an item to click E (by default) to interact with it. This makes you to lose time and smooth gameplay. There are a lot of paths that can lead you to place where you need to be and there's also much space to get through, but the invisible walls don't let you to proceed which makes you to glitch and get stuck a lot in this game.

I'm so torn with this title. After circling it for quite literally years I finally gathered the muster to purchase it and give it a shot. What I discovered was a delightfully in-depth game that held quite a bit of promise. It felt like Minecraft, but more realistic. Plus, of course, the added bonus of graphics that were far more advanced. Most of the crafting system seemed logical and I was able to figure it out without too much help from online tutorials. That being said, I'm not (sadly) not sure I could fully recommend the game to new players. Including myself. See, this title has been around so long that at this point it has become nigh impossible for any newcomer to advance to the role of high-ranking player on any given server. And without a designated single-player mode, this game is left feeling like a reclusive club that refuses to accept new members. Is it fun? Yes. Should you play it? Perhaps, if you can muster up a small group of friends (I'd say around 4-5) that can run around with you and help start something worth protecting. Without said comrades, you'll find yourself hopping from sleeping bag to sleeping bag hoping to steal and hide enough materials to one day construct a small hut that might feature a door....if you're lucky.

TL;DR - (Tireless FPS gameplay) (Brilliant world/character design) (Engaging story) (Very fun co-op) (Unique graohics) (Long, worth the price, but may feel repetitive) (Definitely replayable) (Single player is lonely) (DLCs are great on sale price) (Plenty of violence)
+ Gameplay - The variety of guns, skills, classes and elements will keep you excited about playing simply because there are so many ways to kill your enemies
+ Story/Character/World - Pandora is designed brilliantly: it's so whacky that it's normal. The best way of enjoying the Pandoran experience is to embrace the madness. Comes with some sobering, dark moments, too. You care about derpy allies and learn to hate the seemingly derpy antagonist.
+ Co-op - i practically moved into my buddy's house. Playing with friends makes the game many times more enjoyable because you can revel in your badassadry together, laugh at the craziness together and kill stuff together.
+ Graphics - The cartoonish graphics might take some getting used to, but in the long run, they make the world of BL2 much mroe endearing and less likely to become stale after hours of gameplay
+/- Length/Replay Value - Pretty long single player for an FPS, plenty of side quests. Replay value comes in the form of DLC's, loot hunting and harder game modes. Replay value drops significantly if you don't like the somewhat repetitive gamplay (which won't be a problem if you enjoy the whackiness thrown in with the repetitiveness
+/- Technical Issues - Generally reliable in my experience (with solid but unspectacular specs). I've had some minor trouble with the Cloud Syncing and game files, nothing serious. Haven't experienced in-game tech issues as of yet.
- Single player gets lonely. Pandora is a huge place.
- If you don't like mindless violence as part of your video gaming experience, be warned: BL2 will push your buttons, hard.

I'll be straight with all of you people. This game is in the top ten best games I've ever played, and in the top three shooters in history, hands down. I could rag on about the exciting gameplay, graphical style, addictive nature, intense replayability, and all the other enjoyable aspects that this game has to offer, but you can read that in other reviews. But, oddly enough, with all that said, the gameplay itself, while extremely strong, only made up about 60% of the game for me. It's a fun game, but it's more than that, Borderlands 2 is a living, breathing entity, one that has cohesion, style, and personality on a level that rare in actual people, let alone a video game. I've never before stopped in the middle of a gunfight, and told everyone in the room, "Shut the ♥♥♥♥ up, Handsome Jack is talking."
I've read essays in the past that say that video games are an art form on par with literature and film in terms of storytelling prowess, and they make a compelling argument. Does that mean I'm saying Borderlands 2 is the Citizen Kane of video games? No, it's more like the Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy: a work that's so non-sensical in its absurdity that you can't help but enjoy hearing about its angst over and over again. I can't tell you how many times I've watched Tiny Tina sing "Pop goes the bandit!" while singing along and laughing like a madman. It never gets old. This game is a classic, the kind I'll still be playing twenty years from now while explaining ye-olde gaming to my kids. It overcomes its occasional gameplay issues with overwhelming force of personality. You owe it to yourself to buy this masterpiece. 9.8/10.

This review is negative because I do not want someone who wants a completely unflawed and bug free game experience, to purchase this game in expectance of a perfect survival simulator.
I want to start off with a disclaimer that you should not buy this game in it’s current state unless you know for sure what you are getting and accepting of what it is.
I also want to mention that it has become very hard to play alone due to the developers creating a new loot spawn system where the can make the coast (where you spawn) very barren in terms of loot spawns, and the inland areas (where lots of groups and geared players reside) spawn much better and higher quantities of loot. A positive to this though, is that with the new loot system came an engine revamp, and now the game uses DirectX 11 and a lot more GPU power, causing people to achieve much higher frames than ever before. If you’re reading this review right now and you’re yet to purchase the game, you might be wondering, “Well, what exactly am I getting?” I’ll tell you what you’re getting.
Before I start off, I want to tell you that you should play on servers with a lower ping (how much time it takes for the server to communicate with your computer, measured in milliseconds). There are currently nasty netcode bugs that interrupt almost all parts of the game, however, they can be reduced by playing on a server with lower ping as aforementioned.
You’re purchasing DayZ, an unscripted survival game which has literally infinite possibilities of what can happen during gameplay. You log into a server, and you spawn into the map in a random area in one of the preplanned spawn points. If you open your inventory by pressing Tab, you’ll see that you have basic clothing, a road flare and a rag. Now if you’re an experienced player, you’ll look around and see where you’ve spawned. Most of the time, someone who has more than 300 hours of gameplay can identify where they have spawned, and a player with 1000 hours or more of gameplay can essentially identify where they are instantly, however, this is not you. You are a new player.
The inability to identify where you are may come as frustrating at first. Perhaps you want to get the a military base to pick up some sweet firearms to defend yourself with? This is impossible to do without knowing where you are first, unless you head in the right direction without even realizing it. Know that this is part of the game, and if you play enough you will memorize the map quickly. Memorizing the map may seem difficult, however, it isn’t nearly as daunting as it seems. Over the many lives you will live in DayZ, you will notice that you ‘recognize this place’ more often than not.
Pathfinding is just one of the struggles involved in playing DayZ. Another grand struggle in this amazing game is the threat of fellow survivors. Imagine yourself, all alone running through a thick forest. You think you’re heading to the large western military base, but you don’t know whether you’re heading in the correct direction or not due to your newness to the game. You have a constant feeling of fear as you do not have any weapon in your possession except for your splitting axe. What if somebody with a gun crosses paths with you and poses an extremely unfair threat? What kind of fight would that be? An axe versus a carbine rifle is something you’d never experience in any other game. You heed not at all to the numerous trees that surround you, and you’re very ambitious to get to that military base you’ve heard rumors of. The very basic footstep sounds are annoying you, the constant crunching noise against the ground is enough to make you lose your sanity. The annoyance of your jogging shoes hitting the ground is broken by a distant noise, unmistakably a gunshot. The noise isn’t even far either. Your heart rate picks up as the frenzy of questions pass through your mind. Am I being shot at? If not, then who are they shooting at? You hear another shot, but this time it’s followed by a snapping noise. You’re worst fear has been confirmed, you are being fired upon. You hear another shot and a fleshy impact noise, your screen turns black with a small amount of text displayed which gradually comes into view.
“You are dead”.
That’s right, everything you had worked for on the character, though it may not be much, is now gone. All of those cans of beans you had stored in your taloon backpack now belong to the person who fired upon you. Imagine coming into contact with fate if you had the gear of the person that shot you? That’s where even more pressure comes in, hours and hours of looting, and days of surviving, all leading up to a single bullet fired into your skull. It’s extremely brutal, but that’s the game you’re getting, it’s DayZ.
Permadeath may not be your cup of tea, I mean, who really enjoys losing all of their progress from one idiotic mistake? It’s what makes DayZ what it is, it is known for being a host of extremely rough yet realistic gameplay. I’d like to say that you can avoid these mistakes by simply playing smart, however that isn’t the case.
This brings me back to the point where I brought up playing on servers with good ping. Unfortunately, DayZ has a bit more than it’s unforgiving environment that you have to worry about, the game is victim to lots and lots of bugs. You may find yourself running through a forest one day, your run on top of a rock and think nothing of it. All of a sudden you see the dreaded “You are dead” screen. Why? You didn’t hear any gunshots, and your screen had full color which signifies good health. What happened was one of the netcode bugs. The server’s idea of where you are and your client’s representation can be two very different things. You might have been in an elevated house at one point. The server might still think you’re at that elevation. As soon as you stepped on the rock, the elevation increased a lot in a short amount of time. As soon as you step off of the rock, the server thinks you fell out of the building from earlier which will result in a death.
Another very important example of glitches to bring up are that there are glitches with player movement animation. For instance, a player can be stuck in the swimming animation long after they get out of water. During this period they can pull out guns and use them, leaving only their head exposed, with their body under the ground while they see the screen normally as if they were standing up. Combine this with poor netcode, and it will be hard to hit the player’s head. You will be long dead before you can even hit a shot.
If you are prepared to experience bugs, and are okay with them, then by all means, purchase the game. However, to the general people who want an unflawed experience with no bugs, I wouldn't recommend this game to you, because at some point you will deal with the bugs that unfortunately come with this beautiful game.

This game is a true amazing experience. Gameplay is well designed in which the story and side mission items are conveniently placed. There are no questions about smooth gameplay and characters with personalities and great introductions to them. This is not another shoot 'em up game, you actually have to make up your strategy along the way and change it according to gameplay differences with each character you choose and enemies you face.
Pros:
+art style
+gameplay design through missions
+characters have personalities
+convenient item placement
Cons:
-robotic and stiff enemy movement
-a lot of invisible walls
DETAILS:
You don't get rewarded for your shooting skill. Let's take a sniper for example. If you want to use a sniper in combination with your character you need to find your enemy's weak spots, and by doing so, you have more chance to survive sparing some ammo. Now, that works for a little while you're around 10-20 lvl. Later the enemies are strong even in their weak spots, and this makes you vulnerable. It doesn't matter if you have a stronger sniper than before. You start to lose ammo and take other guns instead. Now you need to get closer to your enemy because you don't have any progress with sniper. You notice that one weapon doesn't do enough damage to all your enemies (usually in the number of 5-10 and above). You notice that you're low on health and your shield isn't recharging fast enough. This makes you to get to ''fight for your life'' mode and gain some of the health and full shield which beats the purpose of the game. There really shouldn't be flaws like this that gamers exploit.
Besides the game changing flaw, I should really talk about item placement. As I said before, items with which you need to interact or pick are conveniently placed according to storyline. There's one mission in which you need to deliver some packages on time to mailboxes near the shore. Now, in any other game the items would be placed in same distances from another and would waste your time in which the time is of importance. In this game, mailboxes are conveniently placed as they would be in real life, but now time isn't that much important as your ability to get through enemies and find all placed mailboxes (some good designing♥♥♥♥♥♥right there).
The last concern of mine are invisible walls, true enemies of every gamer. Now, this includes the fact that you have to stand exactly in front of an item to click E (by default) to interact with it. This makes you to lose time and smooth gameplay. There are a lot of paths that can lead you to place where you need to be and there's also much space to get through, but the invisible walls don't let you to proceed which makes you to glitch and get stuck a lot in this game.

Borderlands 2 has a near-unlimited variety of awesome guns, which can be used on a great number of fearsome enemies.  Borderlands 2 is all about shooting the same palette-shifted enemies with the same boring weapons.  It brings the best of the Diablo-like action RPGs together with the FPS genre.  It lacks the simplicity of the former, and the skill of the latter.  The game has 4 playable classes, which can use very different playstyles.  All the classes use the same guns, so aside from their unique skill and a few passive bonuses, they all wind up playing about the same.  It has tons of secrets, easter eggs, and rewards for exploration, as well as achievements galore.  It doles out a steady drip of meaningless bonuses, based on a Big-Brother-esque monitoring of everything you do.  It has an amazing variety of environments, and some truly epic boss battles.  It parades you through spots that look spectacular, but really only offer a new sequence of boxes or chest-high walls to hide behind, and the bosses are all repetitive cycles of poking out of cover, unloading your clip, then ducking back to hide from their super attack.
It has a great story with a loathsome villain, to draw the players in.  It has a forgettable story with a cardboard-cutout villain that you're simply told to hate because of what he does off-screen, as well as his persistent audio taunts.  It has wonderful writing, with a dark comedy style that is often hilarious.  It can only muster a few cheap laughs with riffs on tired pop-culture  references and entirely predictable jokes.
Borderlands 2 is a triumph, whose huge sales figures attest to the impact it's had in the games industry.  Borderlands 2 is a trashy, manipulative, cynical appeal to the lowest common denominator, and represents everything that's wrong with modern game design.
Which is it?  Well, that depends on your perspective..

Solid RPG Gameplay Wrapped in Emotion
I admit, when I first launched this game, I did not understand what catapulted it to cult status. The look of the game was a little offputting, given the NES/SNES/Gameboy hybrid art style. The gameplay, though unique in its shoot ’em up style dodging system, felt cumbersome to me. I felt all this as I dredged through the opening, hanging on by a single thread: The characters. And boy, am I glad I stuck around.
The game’s quirky characters take many pages from the Earthbound/Mother series of games as well as little sprinkles from the various RPG series starring Mario. They are full of wit and charm, never knowing what situation you are going to find yourself in next. As funny and odd as they can be, they all seem to be held back by various quirks of their personality or the situation of the monsters underground, delving into some rather dark subplots and events. This is what pulled me through the game. The sprite work itself is beautiful, recalling images of Earthbound as even the most insignificant mob has its own unique sprite bursting with personality. And the best part of the combat system? I don’t have to hurt anyone if choose not to.
The game turns the RPG genre on its head by allowing you to spare all of your foes, largely affecting the  game’s ending depending on how you go about it. As tempting as it can be to just crush all the mobs in front of you, the game pulls at your heartstrings and tempts you to run as a pacifist. This is a game best enjoyed multiple times, though I would recommend the most violent of runs as the last, for maximum effect and other reasons I do not plan on disclosing. As quickly as I fell in love with the characters and plot, the unique dodging system also drew me in despite my initial dislike and dread. The game also contains a gorgeous soundtrack, especially considering that it was all made by a single developer. No single track felt out of place and the boss themes are fantastic. Give it a try beyond the Ruins, and I assure you that you won’t be disappointed by this emotional rollercoaster.
